name: Battleship Petropavlovsk
summary: Petropavlovsk was a Russian Poltava-class battleship and one of the principal ships of the Port Arthur squadron. On 31 March (13 April) 1904 she struck Japanese mines and sank with Vice Admiral Stepan Makarov, members of his staff and most of those aboard.
intro: The final morning of Petropavlovsk has overshadowed the rest of her story. Before becoming the ship on which Makarov died, she was one of three new battleships built in St Petersburg for fleet combat. Her fate helps explain why heavy shells were not the only threat to the Port Arthur squadron: the waters around its own base could be turned into a minefield.

sections.title: Three battleships for the battle line
paragraphs: Petropavlovsk was built at Galerny Island in St Petersburg. Laid down in 1892 and launched in 1894, she still needed fitting out, armament and trials. Together with Poltava and Sevastopol she formed a class of three ships. Reference books call it either the Poltava or the Petropavlovsk class: these are two names for the same group, not two different designs.

A squadron battleship was intended to fight other heavily armed ships as part of a formation. The squadron steamed in line ahead, one ship following another, so that its commander could direct its movement and gunfire. Armour, armament and the ability to keep station therefore mattered as much as an individual ship’s speed. Around the turn of the century Petropavlovsk was sent to the Far East; by the outbreak of war she was an established member of the Port Arthur squadron.

sections.title: Thick armour and two heavy turrets
paragraphs: The main battery comprised four 305-mm guns, two in the forward turret and two aft. The figure 305 gives the diameter of the bore in millimetres. The secondary battery included twelve 152-mm Canet guns: eight in four twin turrets and another four in a broadside battery. Small 47-mm and 37-mm guns were intended chiefly to repel torpedo boats, the small, fast vessels that carried torpedoes.

Petropavlovsk’s main belt of nickel-steel armour reached 406 mm at its thickest point. This did not mean that a forty-centimetre wall enclosed the whole ship. The belt protected a particular section of the side near the waterline; the deck, turrets, ends and underwater hull had different protection. Comparing battleships by their greatest armour thickness alone is therefore misleading, especially when the blow came from below, beyond the belt’s protection.

sections.title: A flagship in the opening weeks
paragraphs: At the start of the war Petropavlovsk carried the flag of the squadron commander, Vice Admiral Oskar Stark. The Japanese night attack of 26–27 January (8–9 February) 1904 damaged Retvizan, Tsesarevich and Pallada. Petropavlovsk remained operational and took part in the ensuing daylight engagement. With two powerful battleships immediately out of action, preserving the squadron’s remaining heavy ships became particularly important.

Stepan Osipovich Makarov arrived on 24 February (8 March) and pressed for more active operations: sorties, reconnaissance and crew training. He soon raised his flag in Petropavlovsk. The battleship herself remained under Captain Nikolai Matveyevich Yakovlev. The admiral directed the fleet, while the captain was responsible for his own ship: two distinct duties came together on the flagship’s deck.

sections.title: The morning of 31 March
paragraphs: On 31 March (13 April) Petropavlovsk left Port Arthur following a clash between Russian and Japanese torpedo craft. The cruiser Bayan was already operating near the place where the destroyer Strashny had been lost. Makarov brought out part of the squadron, then turned back towards the base when the main Japanese force appeared. The previous night the Japanese had laid mines across a route the Russian ships used when manoeuvring off the roadstead.

On the return leg the flagship entered the minefield. An underwater explosion was followed by further explosions inside the ship, and she quickly went down by the bow. Technical reconstructions debate which magazines and charges exploded first. What matters when looking out over the roadstead is the scale of the disaster: a large battleship sank within minutes, leaving almost no time for an organised evacuation. Her side armour could not contain the spreading internal catastrophe.

sections.title: More than sailors aboard
paragraphs: The dead included Makarov, his chief of staff Rear Admiral Mikhail Pavlovich Molas, and the artist Vasily Vasilyevich Vereshchagin. The painter had come to the theatre of war as a visitor, not as a regular member of the crew. His naval education had linked him to the fleet since his youth, but by 1904 he was a world-famous artist who had come to see the war for himself. His presence placed the ship in the history of Russian art as well as naval warfare.

The Central Naval Museum gives approximately 650 dead and 80 survivors. Captain Yakovlev and Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich were among those rescued. Other totals appear in the literature, depending on whether crew, staff and additional people aboard are counted; a rounded museum figure should not be treated as a definitive roll of names. The ship never returned to service. In a single catastrophe, long before the siege ended, Port Arthur lost a battleship, its fleet commander and part of his staff. In 1909–1913 an expedition organised by the Japanese businessman Tsunenosuke Sakurai examined the wreck. According to A. V. Okorokov’s research, divers recovered the remains of six Russian sailors, buried in Port Arthur’s military cemetery in 1913. Documents found with the remains identified Molas among them. Makarov was not among those identified. The ship’s underwater history continued, but the claim that she was subsequently broken up completely remains a theory, not proof that the wreck site has been fully investigated.

name: Battleship Retvizan
summary: Retvizan was built for Russia in Philadelphia and reached Port Arthur in 1903. She survived a torpedo hit on the first night of the war and the Battle of the Yellow Sea, then sank in the harbour under siege fire. Raised by Japan, she served again as Hizen.
intro: In the opening weeks of the war Retvizan found herself in an unusual position: a battleship aground at the entrance to her own harbour, yet still fighting. Her heavy guns helped defend the channel through which she herself would eventually have to return. It was hardly the start envisaged when one of the squadron’s newest battleships was ordered.

sections.title: An American hull with Russian guns
paragraphs: The contract went to William Cramp & Sons of Philadelphia. Construction began in 1899, and the ship was launched in 1900, but delivery and final adjustments took longer. Retvizan was not a standard American battleship simply repainted for Russia: the design combined the requirements of Russia’s Naval Technical Committee with solutions adopted by Cramp’s yard. Her artillery was manufactured in Russia.

The trials dispel any notion that a new ship was necessarily a finished machine. Captain Eduard Nikolayevich Shchensnovich’s report discussed unfinished work, calculation of the final payment and difficulties achieving the contracted 18 knots. In October 1901 the New-York Tribune separately reported Retvizan’s arrival at the Brooklyn Navy Yard for further hull work. Outwardly the battleship looked complete, but acceptance involved many specific checks.

sections.title: The battleship’s armament
paragraphs: Four Obukhov 305-mm guns, with barrels 40 calibres long, formed the main battery in two twin turrets. Twelve 152-mm Canet guns occupied casemates, protected compartments in the broadside battery. Twenty 75-mm guns and smaller weapons were intended primarily against torpedo boats. This was the outfit at the start of the war. Later, guns and men were sent ashore for the land defences, so the nominal armament no longer matched what remained aboard.

The armour belt reached 229 mm at its thickest, as did the turret armour. Two steam engines and 24 Niclausse water-tube boilers provided propulsion. Trials examined more than power and speed: they tested the foundations under heavy-turret firing and the ship’s behaviour when damaged. Substantial armour did not remove the need to detect flooding promptly, isolate damaged compartments and keep the pumps supplied with power.

sections.title: A torpedo hit and an improvised battery
paragraphs: After crossing the Atlantic and serving in the Baltic, Retvizan reached Port Arthur in spring 1903. On the first night of the war, 26–27 January (8–9 February) 1904, a Japanese torpedo struck the port bow. Contemporary Russian documents often called a torpedo a “self-propelled mine”; this was not the stationary moored mine that would later sink Petropavlovsk. The damaged battleship grounded near the harbour entrance.

There she became a forward floating battery. On the night preceding 11 (24) February, Japanese steamers attempted to sink themselves in the channel and bottle up the Russian squadron. Retvizan helped repel the attack. Stark’s report of 18 February describes her gunfire, the positions of the sunken steamers and the scuttling equipment found aboard them. Success had a practical meaning: the exit remained open to Russian ships. Shchensnovich received the Order of St George, fourth class.

sections.title: Turning towards the Japanese line
paragraphs: After repairs Retvizan resumed operations with the squadron. On 28 July (10 August) 1904 she took part in the attempted breakout to Vladivostok and the Battle of the Yellow Sea, following the flagship Tsesarevich. When Rear Admiral Wilgelm Vitgeft was killed and damage to the flagship’s steering disrupted the Russian column, Shchensnovich turned his battleship towards the Japanese ships.

The captain later explained that he intended to ram the enemy. This is a participant’s account of his intention, not a description of a completed ramming attack: the approach did not end in a collision. Shchensnovich was concussed, and Retvizan turned away and returned to Port Arthur. The episode is often presented as a spectacular victory in its own right. Its actual outcome was more limited and more painful: the battleship survived the gunnery action, but the squadron’s breakout failed and its ships were back in their besieged base.

sections.title: A second career under another name
paragraphs: In autumn the ship supported the fortress’s defenders with gunfire, men and weapons transferred ashore. Japanese siege artillery badly damaged her in December 1904, and she settled on the harbour bottom. Sinking in shallow water did not necessarily mean that hull and machinery were lost for ever. Before the surrender Russian sailors inflicted further damage on essential equipment to make the ship harder for the enemy to use.

The Japanese raised her in 1905 and, after extensive reconstruction, commissioned her in 1908 as Hizen. Early in the First World War she joined the search for Admiral Spee’s German squadron; later she appeared at Vladivostok during the Japanese intervention. Reclassified as a coast-defence ship in 1921, she was subsequently disarmed and removed from the navy list. Her final role was as a floating target: in July 1924 the former Retvizan was sunk during exercises in the Bungo Strait. She had outlived Russian Port Arthur by almost twenty years.

name: Armoured cruiser Bayan
summary: The first armoured cruiser Bayan, built in France, served at Port Arthur in 1903–1904. She carried out reconnaissance, covered light forces and supported the fortress’s defence. Sunk in the harbour, she was raised by Japan and continued her career as Aso.
intro: Bayan had two distinct naval careers, and another Russian ship later bore the same name. The defender of Port Arthur was the first, French-built cruiser; the Baltic Bayan of the First World War came later. By then the former Port Arthur ship was already sailing under the Japanese flag. A name without a date and place of service can easily lead into somebody else’s biography.

sections.title: A scout with armour
paragraphs: The requirements for a new cruiser took shape in 1897. She was to serve with the battleship squadron: scouting, supporting its light forces and joining the general action when necessary. Speed alone would not suffice. She was given a side armour belt and protected heavy guns. Such vessels were called armoured cruisers: unlike protected cruisers, they carried armour on the sides as well as the deck.

The order went to Forges et Chantiers de la Méditerranée at La Seyne, near Toulon. Work began late in 1898; the formal laying-down ceremony took place only after the hull had already risen substantially on the slipway. Launch followed in 1900, but trials and correction of defects continued until the end of 1902. Ordering abroad did not eliminate delays: drawings changed, components and armour were tested and rejected, machinery adjusted. Operational service was still some way off.

sections.title: Two eight-inch guns and eight six-inch guns
paragraphs: The main armament comprised two Obukhov 203-mm guns with barrels 45 calibres long, one in the forward turret and one aft. “Eight inches” and “203 millimetres” describe the same calibre. Eight 152-mm Canet guns were mounted along the sides. There were also twenty 75-mm guns, smaller weapons and torpedo tubes. This was a small main battery for heavy combat, but the cruiser’s task differed from a battleship’s.

Design speed was about 21 knots, or approximately 39 kilometres an hour. Twenty-six Belleville boilers supplied steam to two triple-expansion engines. The main belt was up to 200 mm thick and the turrets had 150 mm of armour. This protection allowed her to accept the risks of operating close to the enemy, but did not turn the cruiser into a small battleship. Every sortie also depended on the range, the nature of any hits and the ability to keep moving.

sections.title: In time for the war
paragraphs: In 1903 Bayan visited the Baltic before sailing to the Far East with the battleship Tsesarevich. Both reached Port Arthur in autumn. The cruiser was commanded by Captain Robert Nikolayevich Viren. Her crew had little time to become familiar with the new theatre before the Russo-Japanese War began.

In the opening weeks Bayan was already scouting with Askold and Novik. The fleet had to investigate reports of enemy ships and possible landings, cover destroyers and watch the approaches to its base. Not every sortie ended in combat: sometimes an alarm proved false. This was nevertheless the scout’s everyday work. The cruiser was there to bring information to the command, rather than seek a fight at any price and leave the squadron without eyes at sea.

sections.title: Two mornings near the harbour entrance
paragraphs: On 31 March (13 April) 1904 Bayan went to the scene of the destroyer Strashny’s last action. She exchanged fire and rescued five sailors still in the water. Petropavlovsk sank with Makarov that same day. The two events formed part of one operation off Port Arthur, but they were separate episodes: the cruiser did not strike a mine with the flagship and returned to base.

Her own encounter with a mine came on 14 (27) July, when a detachment was returning after supporting troops ashore. Bayan took on water but remained able to steam and reached the harbour under her own power. Dockyard repairs followed, keeping her out of the force that attempted to break through to Vladivostok on 28 July (10 August). Some guns removed during repairs were used to reinforce other ships: in a besieged base a working gun was needed immediately, even if its own ship was still in dock.

sections.title: Still part of the defence
paragraphs: Bayan’s crew also helped defend Port Arthur on land. Sailors manned guns transferred ashore, worked on the fortifications and served in the garrison. In the final months of the siege the distinction between a ship’s company and the defenders of the forts grew increasingly blurred. Even when unable to put to sea, the cruiser continued to supply the fortress with artillery, ammunition and men.

In late November Old Style, already December in the Gregorian calendar, Japanese siege guns badly damaged her in the Eastern Basin. She settled on the bottom after the bombardments; her crew continued removing whatever equipment and ammunition remained accessible. Before the fortress surrendered, further damage was inflicted on the cruiser’s machinery and equipment. This interrupted her service for a long time, but the shallow harbour gave the victor the prospect of raising her. Bayan’s history did not end with Russian Port Arthur.

sections.title: From cruiser to minelayer
paragraphs: The Japanese raised the ship in 1905 and rebuilt her at Maizuru. In 1908 she returned to service as the armoured cruiser Aso. Boilers and armament were replaced during reconstruction, so specifications for her Russian guns cannot automatically be applied to photographs bearing the new name. Her superstructure and gun arrangement also changed later.

In 1920 Aso was converted into a minelayer, a ship equipped to lay naval minefields. She was removed from the navy list in 1930 and sunk as a gunnery target in 1932. A cruiser that had ended the Russo-Japanese War on the bottom of Port Arthur harbour thus served another state for more than two further decades. Her later career is particularly clear when two photographs are compared: the Russian four-funnel scout and the reconstructed Japanese ship.

name: Battleship Mikasa
summary: A British-built Japanese battleship and Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō’s flagship in the war of 1904–1905. Mikasa fought against the Port Arthur squadron and at Tsushima; after a long career and two restorations she became a memorial ship at Yokosuka.
intro: Mikasa survived the war with Russia, sank after peace had been signed, returned to service and then nearly disappeared after becoming a memorial. Today she can be visited at Yokosuka, a Japanese naval port south of Tokyo. Yet half a century of history separates Tōgō’s bridge from the present museum: an explosion, repairs, an earthquake and the reconstruction of an almost vanished silhouette.

sections.title: A Japanese order at a British yard
paragraphs: The battleship was built in Britain by Vickers at Barrow-in-Furness. She was laid down on 24 January 1899, launched on 8 November 1900 and commissioned on 1 March 1902. These dates use the Gregorian, or New Style, calendar followed in Japan and Britain. Mikasa completed Japan’s programme of six battleships ordered from British yards. Together with armoured cruisers, they formed the core of the fleet with which Japan entered the war against Russia.

The order illustrates how the naval arms race worked. Japan strengthened its fleet through British industry; Russia also bought warships abroad. The rivals were preparing for war in East Asia, but many of their future ships were taking shape on European and American slipways. A national flag at the stern did not necessarily mean a nationally built hull and machinery.

sections.title: Four heavy guns and a battery between them
paragraphs: Mikasa belonged to the generation of battleships that preceded the dreadnoughts. Her main battery consisted of four 305-mm guns in two twin turrets, one forward and one aft. Between them stood a battery of fourteen 152-mm guns. A casemate was a protected compartment with an opening in the ship’s side, allowing a gun to fire out while sheltering its crew. Armour protected the sides and vital internal areas: this was a ship intended to fight in line alongside other battleships.

Twenty-five Belleville boilers supplied steam to two triple-expansion engines driving two propellers. The museum gives a power of 15 000 horsepower and a speed of 18 knots. A knot is one nautical mile per hour. For a heavy ship of the period this was part of her fighting capability, but not a promise that she could maintain it regardless of machinery condition, coal load or sea state. A specification describes the ship under stated conditions, not every day of her service.

sections.title: The flagship off Port Arthur
paragraphs: At the end of December 1903 Mikasa became flagship of the Combined Fleet, carrying Tōgō and his staff. The captain was responsible for the battleship and her crew, while the admiral commanded the fleet: two different chains of responsibility met on one deck. In 1904–1905 Mikasa’s captain was Hikojirō Ijichi; Tōgō’s staff included Tomosaburō Katō and the operations officer Akiyama Saneyuki.

Mikasa’s connection with Port Arthur was direct: she operated against the Russian squadron based there. On 27 January (9 February) 1904 she took part in the daylight action off the fortress, and on 28 July (10 August) in the Battle of the Yellow Sea. The Russian ships were attempting to break out from Port Arthur to Vladivostok; the Japanese fleet sought to stop them. Mikasa was no observation post safely in the distance. The Japanese flagship came under fire, sustained damage and needed repairs.

sections.title: Life between battles
paragraphs: Keeping a fleet almost continuously off an enemy coast required fuel, maintenance and food. Military historian Akinori Ishihara uses Japanese records to examine Mikasa’s menu for 30 May 1904. The ship was then at an island forward base south of the Liaodong Peninsula, not inside Port Arthur harbour. Lunch included rice and barley with canned salmon and hijiki seaweed; supper comprised hardtack and beef with potatoes.

According to Ishihara, spoiled canned salmon caused food poisoning in 156 people. That is a figure for illness, not deaths. It is a thoroughly naval detail: fighting efficiency also depended on those who loaded food, monitored its storage and prepared meals. A battle could be decided upon on the flagship’s bridge, but several hundred people had to be fed every day, whatever the admiral’s plans.

sections.title: Victory, an explosion and a return to service
paragraphs: On 14–15 (27–28) May 1905 Tōgō commanded the Japanese fleet from Mikasa at the Battle of Tsushima. His opponent was the Russian squadron that had sailed from the Baltic. This was a different stage of the war: Port Arthur had already surrendered, and Vladivostok remained the Russian fleet’s intended destination. Mikasa was hit again but survived. Her later importance as a national memorial was linked above all to Tsushima.

A few days after the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed, on 12 September 1905 New Style, a fire and magazine explosion sank the battleship at anchor in Sasebo. A U.S. Naval Institute article gives 251 crew members killed; early newspaper reports offered other, provisional totals. Raised in 1906, she returned to service after repairs in 1908. During the First World War she served in coastal defence; later she helped support Japan’s presence off Siberia. The victor of Tsushima continued to age like any other warship.

sections.title: The memorial needed saving too
paragraphs: The Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 limited the major powers’ battle fleets. The old battleship was removed from naval service, and preserving her as a memorial required the treaty signatories’ consent. After damage in the Great Kantō Earthquake, she was moved to her present site in 1925. The memorial was formally opened on 12 November 1926.

After the Second World War Mikasa lost her turrets, guns, bridges, funnels and masts. Entertainment facilities were installed inside, then fell into decline themselves. A surviving hull did not mean a surviving ship. A new restoration was completed on 27 May 1961. Today’s Mikasa is therefore a historical hull with reconstructed parts of her appearance and a museum exhibition. She was never renamed or transferred to another navy: the name survived with the hull, although her purpose changed completely.

name: Cruiser Novik
summary: A fast Russian second-class cruiser built in Germany and one of the most active ships of the Port Arthur squadron. After escaping from Port Arthur she was scuttled off Sakhalin, then raised by Japan and served as Suzuya until her removal from the navy list in 1913.
intro: Novik was meant to see farther than the squadron and reach places a heavy battleship could not reach in time. That was why her engines and boilers occupied so much of the design. At Port Arthur the small cruiser was constantly in demand for reconnaissance, fighting torpedo craft and supporting troops near the coast. Yet her story ended far from the fortress, and her Russian name was followed by a Japanese one.

sections.title: A scout for the Far East
paragraphs: The ship was ordered under the naval programme of 1898, adopted to strengthen Russia’s fleet in the Far East. It called for a cruiser of about 3000 tonnes to scout for the squadron, support friendly torpedo craft and fight enemy boats. This was a distinct role; comparing her artillery with a battleship’s without considering her purpose would make little sense. Novik was designed above all for speed and the ability to operate frequently on detached duties for the squadron.

The contract went to the German firm Schichau. The hull was built at Danzig, now Gdańsk, and the machinery at Elbing, now Elbląg. Actual construction preceded the ceremonial laying down: by the official date the hull had already reached the armoured deck. Launched in 1900, the cruiser then underwent lengthy trials and correction of defects. Final acceptance was completed in spring 1902. In May she reached Kronstadt, sailed for the Pacific in autumn and arrived at Port Arthur in April 1903.

sections.title: The price of speed in weight and space
paragraphs: Three steam engines drove three propellers; twelve water-tube boilers supplied their steam. Over five runs at the end of her trials, the cruiser averaged 25.08 knots at approximately 17 800 horsepower. Figures of 26 knots also appear in the literature for individual trials. These are different measures. The highest cannot simply be selected and treated as a speed the cruiser was obliged to sustain after months of war without a proper refit.

The term “protected cruiser” describes her armour arrangement. There was no belt along the ship’s side; instead, an internal armoured deck with sloping sides shielded the engines and other vital spaces. Her main weapons were six 120-mm guns, supplemented by small-calibre artillery and torpedo tubes. Against torpedo craft this was a much heavier armament than a boat’s own. Against a large cruiser armed with six-inch guns, it meant a significant disadvantage.

sections.title: A cruiser always in demand
paragraphs: At the start of the war Novik was commanded by Commander Nikolai Ottovich Essen. In the daylight battle of 27 January (9 February) 1904 he closed with the Japanese ships. A 203-mm shell damaged the stern and steering compartment, forcing the cruiser out of action and into dock. Lieutenant Andrey Shter, who served aboard, observed plainly that courage did not turn a light scout into a ship fit for a fleet gunnery battle.

Admiral Stepan Makarov’s arrival brought more active fleet operations. On one sortie Makarov raised his flag in Novik in an attempt to help the destroyer Steregushchy. This did not make the admiral a permanent member of her ship’s company. In March Maximilian Fyodorovich Schultz took over the cruiser, while Essen moved to the battleship Sevastopol. Novik continued putting to sea, escorting destroyers and firing on Japanese troops along the coast. Tahe Bay, east of Port Arthur, became one of the places where she supported the land front.

sections.title: From the Yellow Sea around Japan
paragraphs: On 28 July (10 August) 1904 the Port Arthur squadron sailed in an attempt to reach Vladivostok. Its formation broke down after the Battle of the Yellow Sea. Novik followed the cruiser Askold south and escaped the action. But engines and boilers already needed attention, and coal was short. Instead of a direct voyage to the Russian base, she had to put into Qingdao, a German-held port on the Chinese coast.

Staying in a neutral port risked internment: disarmament and withdrawal from the war until its end. Schultz decided to continue. The cruiser rounded Japan on its eastern side, hoping to reach Vladivostok through the La Pérouse Strait between Hokkaido and Sakhalin. First she needed another supply of coal. Her next stop was therefore Korsakov Post on southern Sakhalin. Speed had helped her escape one battle; it did not cancel fuel consumption or the wear on machinery during the voyage that followed.

sections.title: The final action and the crew’s journey
paragraphs: On 7 (20) August near Korsakov Post, Novik fought the Japanese cruiser Tsushima. Damage forced her back. Water was entering the after compartments, damaged machinery limited her speed and another Japanese cruiser, Chitose, was nearby. Schultz ordered his ship scuttled in shallow water. There was still hope of raising her later, since Korsakov Post remained Russian. The next day Chitose shelled the already submerged hull.

The men outlived the ship. Some remained on Sakhalin to salvage equipment and remove guns, while the main body headed north towards Alexandrovsk Post. According to Shter’s diary, eight officers and 270 ratings set out on 17 (30) August. The ship’s musicians refused to abandon their instruments and carried them along. Sorties from Port Arthur had given way to a long journey overland: officers now had to arrange packs, food and a route for men who no longer had a ship.

sections.title: Suzuya and another Novik
paragraphs: The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred southern Sakhalin to Japan. The Japanese raised the cruiser in 1906, repaired her and commissioned her as Suzuya, rendered in more than one way in Russian literature. During reconstruction the first boiler room was not restored to its original condition, and the forward funnel was removed. The armament changed too. A photograph of a two-funnel Japanese ship therefore shows a later stage in the same hull’s life, not the appearance of Novik at Port Arthur.

The former Russian cruiser remained on the Japanese navy list until 1913 and was then sold for scrap. She never returned to the Russian fleet. In Russia, a new turbine-powered destroyer associated with Essen and the Baltic Fleet received the name Novik. That was a different ship, later renamed Yakov Sverdlov. The Port Arthur cruiser’s sequence of names is shorter: Novik—Suzuya. Keeping them distinct matters in both texts and photographs: the celebrated service of one must not quietly extend the biography of the other.

name: Cruiser Varyag
summary: An American-built Russian protected cruiser that served with the squadron based at Port Arthur. Her famous battle took place elsewhere, at Chemulpo in Korea on 27 January (9 February) 1904. She later served Japan as Sōya, returned to Russia and ended her career off Scotland.
intro: “Varyag” and “scuttled by her crew” are usually placed together, as though the ship vanished after Chemulpo. Yet the hull was raised, repaired and used for many more years under another flag. Her story connects an American yard, a Russian base in China, a Korean port, Japanese training service and a final voyage towards the Scottish coast. The song preserved one day; the ship had a history before and after it.

sections.title: An American cruiser for a Russian squadron
paragraphs: Varyag was built by William Cramp & Sons in Philadelphia. The order formed part of Russia’s 1898 programme to strengthen its fleet in the Far East. The ship was launched in 1899, and the St Andrew’s ensign was raised early in 1901. After trials and correction of defects, she sailed to Kronstadt and then towards the Pacific. She reached Port Arthur in 1902.

She was a large scout and a cruiser for operations on sea communications, not a battleship. With a normal displacement of approximately 6500 tonnes, she carried twelve 152-mm Canet guns. An armoured deck protected vital spaces internally, but there was no armour belt along the waterline. The main guns stood in open positions without turret protection: fragments could strike their crews even when no hole threatened the ship’s buoyancy. A strong cruiser battery did not make its men invulnerable.

sections.title: Speed in the tables and at sea
paragraphs: Two triple-expansion steam engines drove two propellers, supplied by thirty Niclausse boilers. During acceptance trials the cruiser achieved about 23 knots. Combined with twelve six-inch guns, this promised a powerful and fast ship. The auxiliary battery included twelve 75-mm guns, smaller pieces, Baranovsky landing guns and six torpedo tubes. The landing guns could also be used by a party put ashore.

In service the boilers and engines repeatedly needed repairs. Recorded trial speed was not the same as the speed a worn installation could sustain at sea. Historian Andrey Gushchin emphasises this difference when comparing specialist studies and participants’ recollections. In his account, technical condition restricted the cruiser’s capabilities. But a general history of defects cannot establish one exact speed for every minute of the subsequent battle, or explain its entire outcome solely through boiler design.

sections.title: From Port Arthur to duty with the envoy
paragraphs: Before the war Varyag belonged to the Russian squadron based at Port Arthur. Her service included voyages, repairs and visits to foreign ports. Vsevolod Fyodorovich Rudnev, who took command, had previously served as senior assistant to the chief of Port Arthur’s naval port. The cruiser’s links with the fortress were therefore both organisational and personal. Her best-known battle, however, belongs on another map.

At the outbreak of war Varyag and the gunboat Koreets were at Chemulpo, now Incheon, on Korea’s west coast. They were station ships: warships posted to a foreign port to represent their country and support its diplomatic mission. Ships of other powers were there too. The neutral roadstead was not a Russian naval base. Returning to Port Arthur required following the channel out to sea, while a Japanese squadron under Rear Admiral Sotokichi Uriū already controlled the approaches.

sections.title: Battle off a Korean port
paragraphs: On 27 January (9 February) 1904 Rudnev received a demand to leave the roadstead; otherwise Uriū threatened to attack in the port. The Russian ships sailed out and fought. Facing them was a force of six cruisers and eight torpedo boats, including the armoured cruiser Asama. The narrow, difficult channel restricted freedom to manoeuvre. Varyag was hit, fires broke out, the hull was holed and men were killed and wounded. The breakout failed.

In his report Rudnev described the death of rangefinding officer Alexei Nirod and the wounding of Pavel Gubonin, who continued to command his gun division. Rangefinders measured the distance to the enemy; their work was as necessary for accurate fire as the operation of the guns themselves. Rudnev was also concussed. The Russian ships returned to the roadstead, and their crews were transferred to neutral vessels. Koreets was blown up; Varyag was scuttled by opening sea valves. This prevented the ship from passing immediately into enemy hands, but did not destroy the hull beyond recovery.

sections.title: Raised and renamed Sōya
paragraphs: The Japanese raised Varyag in 1905. After repairs she entered their navy as Sōya, a name rendered in several ways in Russian, and served as a training cruiser. A new flag and name continued the life of the same hull. Training service required the engines and shipboard systems to be maintained; this was more than keeping a trophy tied to a quay.

During the First World War Russia and Japan were allies. In 1916 the Russian government bought the cruiser back together with two other former Russian warships. Her name Varyag was restored. She made the long passage from Vladivostok to Kola Bay and joined the Arctic Ocean Flotilla. A ship built for the Pacific was needed at the opposite end of the country. In February 1917 she sailed to Britain for repairs, but never returned to her former service.

sections.title: The final shore was Scottish
paragraphs: After the revolution the ship came under British control. The Central Naval Museum dates her requisition to December 1917; sale for breaking up followed. While being towed to the breakers, Varyag grounded on rocks off the Scottish coast. She was broken up at the wreck site in the 1920s. Popular accounts often merge the grounding, destruction of the hull and completion of dismantling into a single “date of loss”, producing different years.

Material remains later became museum objects and memorial relics. Savino in the Tula region has a museum devoted to Captain Rudnev, bringing together family possessions and fragments of the ship found off Scotland. For Port Arthur, Varyag remains part of the story of the squadron that went to war in 1904. But the battle at Chemulpo, Japanese service and voyage north have geographies of their own. Preserving those distinctions restores the full biography of a ship that one famous song could never encompass.

name: Obukhov 305-mm/40 gun, Pattern 1895
summary: The main battery of many Russian pre-dreadnought battleships, including Petropavlovsk and Retvizan. Developed in the early 1890s, the gun continued its career in Soviet coastal defence after its service at sea.
intro: In photographs of a battleship, the eye is often drawn to its two large turrets, one forward and one aft. They housed the weapons with which the ship was expected to face an enemy battleship. For Russian ships of the Port Arthur squadron, this often meant the twelve-inch gun of 40 calibres in length. The compact designation “305/40” stands for an entire generation of the fleet.

sections.title: Why twelve inches was retained
paragraphs: In 1891 the Naval Technical Committee considered a practical question: could the main calibre of new ships be reduced? Lighter guns promised lighter mountings and faster fire. The committee decided, however, that too much projectile power would be lost. Twelve inches was retained, but a new gun had to be designed.

The principal designer was artillery engineer Anton Brink, and the manufacturer the Obukhov Steel Works. The design took shape in winter 1891–1892, with trials in 1895. The French Canet system helped the Russians develop a new breech mechanism, but this did not make the whole gun a French licensed model. It had its own design history.

sections.title: What 305 and 40 mean
paragraphs: The exact calibre was 304.8 mm, or twelve British inches. “40 calibres” expresses length as a multiple of the bore diameter: about 12.2 m. This is not the gun’s full external length with all projecting parts. The convention allows the proportions of guns of different calibres to be compared, but by itself says nothing about range or fighting value.

During the Russo-Japanese War the gun used shells weighing 331.7 kg, relatively light for this calibre. The later Pattern 1911 shell weighed 470.9 kg. Both figures appear in references for the same gun, but the second must not be carried back into an account of a battle in 1904. A ship’s weapons changed over time, and so did their ammunition.

sections.title: The heavy guns of the Port Arthur squadron
paragraphs: Petropavlovsk, Poltava, Sevastopol, Retvizan and Tsesarevich each carried four in two twin turrets. The same main gun thus appeared on ships differing considerably in age, protection and layout. They shared the gun, but not necessarily the turrets or ammunition-handling machinery.

That distinction matters for the rate of fire. Time passed while heavy ammunition came up from the magazines and the mounting returned to its loading position. A gun’s quoted firing rate is not the number of aimed rounds a ship could actually fire in battle. Judging the squadron’s performance by one specification would be convenient, but misleading.

sections.title: After the battleships
paragraphs: The Russo-Japanese War did not end the design’s history. The guns remained aboard ships that fought in the First World War; improvements to their mountings shortened the loading cycle. Later, removed barrels were stored, and some found a new use in coastal defence.

In the USSR six 305-mm/40 guns were fitted to TM-2-12 railway mountings and sent to the Far East. A photograph is easily miscaptioned here: the railway carriage belongs to another era and another mounting, although its barrel originated with late nineteenth-century battleships. The ships went to the breakers, while their main guns remained in service.

name: Canet 152-mm/45 gun, Pattern 1892
summary: A French-designed six-inch gun that became a widespread weapon of the Russian fleet and coastal batteries. At Port Arthur it connected the squadron at sea with the defence of the fortress.
intro: Canet’s name appears constantly in lists of Port Arthur’s armament. Familiarity can obscure the object itself: a long barrel, a shell weighing more than forty kilograms and a crew repeatedly serving a heavy weapon. It was one of the Russian squadron’s most familiar modern guns. It was needed ashore as well.

sections.title: A French design made in Russia
paragraphs: In 1891 a Russian delegation was shown quick-firing guns by the French engineer Gustave Canet. The navy purchased a licence, and production began at the Obukhov Works in 1892. The French surname remained the system’s name, although most Russian sailors handled domestically manufactured guns.

Rapid fire depended on the whole system: breech, recoil mechanism, mounting and ammunition supply. After a shot, the moving part of the gun recoiled and returned, rather than the entire heavy mounting with its crew. For contemporaries, this arrangement mattered as much as an increase in calibre.

sections.title: Six inches does not identify the model
paragraphs: Six inches equals 152.4 mm. A length of 45 calibres corresponds to approximately 6.86 m, helping to convey the gun’s proportions. But “six-inch” alone is not enough: Port Arthur also had older guns of that calibre which differed considerably from the Canet.

A typical older shell weighed 41.4 kg. On Bayan, 152-mm guns occupied casemates, armoured compartments with firing ports. Other ships used different mountings. These differences affected crew protection, available elevation and ammunition handling; the same barrel could have different capabilities on two ships.

sections.title: One system afloat and ashore
paragraphs: Canet guns formed the secondary batteries of Russian battleships and the principal armament of several cruisers. On Varyag they were the main battery; on Bayan they supplemented eight-inch turrets. “Main” and “secondary” describe a weapon’s place in a particular ship’s armament, not an immutable quality of the gun itself.

At the outbreak of war Port Arthur had twenty coastal six-inch Canet guns, but A. Denisov and Yu. Perechnev’s table lists only fifteen mounted in batteries. The remaining five were intended for Battery No. 16, armed in late February 1904. Guns delivered were therefore not automatically guns ready for action. The same list has a separate entry for older six-inch guns weighing 190 poods: the two rows must not be combined.

sections.title: A long life with alterations
paragraphs: Record firing rates in a handbook do not describe hours of combat. Shells had to come up from the magazines, crews tired and machinery suffered damage. Ammunition and loading arrangements changed over the years too. The range of a later coastal mounting should not be attributed to a ship of 1904.

Guns of this family served in the First World War and the Russian Civil War, and remained in Soviet coastal defence. A separate branch continued in Finland, where inherited Russian guns were modified to improve the mountings’ capabilities and later received new barrels. A Finnish museum Canet can therefore look noticeably different from the gun served by sailors at Port Arthur. The origins are shared, but these are different stages in the system’s life.

name: Obukhov 203-mm/45 gun
summary: An eight-inch gun designed by Anton Brink and used on Russian armoured cruisers. In the Port Arthur squadron it formed Bayan’s main battery.
intro: Bayan had only two large turrets, each with one eight-inch gun. Beside a battleship’s four heavy guns, that may look modest. But the cruiser was built for a different role: scouting for the squadron, supporting light forces and fighting cruisers. Her main battery needs to be considered alongside that purpose.

sections.title: A Russian eight-inch gun
paragraphs: In 1892 Anton Brink designed a new eight-inch gun at the Obukhov Works, drawing on experience gained with the six-inch Canet. That connection does not justify giving every Russian gun of the period the same French name. The eight-inch system had its own design and breech mechanism.

“Pattern 1892” is a common designation in the literature, while 1895 appears as the year it entered service. These refer to different stages and need not contradict each other; NavWeaps places both dates side by side. The designation “203-mm/45” remains the same whichever stage of development a reference book’s compiler means.

sections.title: Between six and twelve inches
paragraphs: The exact calibre was 203.2 mm. Forty-five calibres gives a length of about 9.14 m. Barrel and breech weighed approximately 12.18 tonnes: the gun itself, not its turret with armour, drives and ammunition handling. A ship carried a much larger and heavier system around the gun to make it work.

The older eight-inch shell weighed 87.8 kg, more than twice the weight of the older six-inch Canet shell. This helps explain why the cruiser needed different calibres. Yet weight alone is not a ready-made assessment of a hit: shell construction, fuze, the obstacle struck and the circumstances of firing also matter.

sections.title: Bayan’s turrets
paragraphs: On the first Bayan, which arrived at Port Arthur in 1903, two 203-mm guns occupied single turrets forward and aft. This protected the crews and preserved heavy fire ahead and astern. Beneath the turrets were magazines and machinery to bring up ammunition.

The speed of that supply was discussed during design. According to Rafail Melnikov’s study, in March 1898 the Naval Technical Committee objected to an ammunition hoist taking 30–40 seconds instead of the expected 10–15, and required at least two rounds per minute. This was a design requirement, not proof of Bayan’s sustained firing rate in the battles of 1904. The distinction matters: the committee’s wish still had to be made to work in machinery.

sections.title: Cruiser guns after 1905
paragraphs: The model also armed Rossiya and Gromoboi, which operated from Vladivostok. Their deck mounts were not identical to Bayan’s turrets. A shared barrel type did not give ships the same number of guns, crew protection or broadside capability.

Production continued for the later Bayan-class cruisers. During the First World War, eight-inch guns were used to reinforce older ships and coastal batteries. New, heavier shells appeared. Thus one system acquires different entries for range and projectile weight. Port Arthur concerns its early form; later service demonstrates the design’s longevity, but does not allow the armament of 1904 to be improved retrospectively.

name: Elswick (Armstrong) 305-mm/40 gun
summary: A British twelve-inch system carried by Japanese battleships, including Mikasa during the Russo-Japanese War. The family later received the Japanese designation 41st Year Type, which should not be applied as a contemporary name in 1904.
intro: Mikasa was built by Vickers, but that does not mean every part of her armament came from the same firm. A warship brought together the products of different manufacturers. Her four principal guns belonged to the Elswick family, British weapons that became the basis of Japan’s new battleship armament.

sections.title: A British gun for Japan
paragraphs: Elswick was the centre of Armstrong’s artillery manufacturing. Fred Jane’s naval reference book, published in 1904, describes Japan’s adoption of Elswick guns and explicitly includes Mikasa among the ships with twelve-inch guns of 40 calibres in length. Contemporary testimony thus helps distinguish the shipbuilder from the origin of the weapon.

Specialist literature identifies the family as EOC Patterns G and G¹. Resemblance to the British twelve-inch Mark IX does not make them the same model: the export weapon had features of its own. “British twelve-inch gun” is therefore too broad for precise comparison, just as a turret’s silhouette alone cannot establish the model.

sections.title: Four barrels in two turrets
paragraphs: Twelve inches equals 304.8 mm, usually rounded to 305 mm. “40 calibres” describes the barrel’s proportions, not the number of shots or range. The distinction is particularly important here: Mikasa later carried longer twelve-inch guns which must not be substituted in an account of the Russo-Japanese War.

During the war she had two twin mountings, one forward and one aft. The Mikasa museum confirms four main guns of 40 calibres. The shell weighed about 386 kg; the museum’s popular explanation rounds this to 400 kg. Specifying the precision is more useful than arguing over a few kilograms: the museum’s rounded figure and the reference weight describe the same scale, not two different shell models.

sections.title: The flagship’s main battery
paragraphs: In 1904 Mikasa was Admiral Tōgō’s flagship and took part in operations off Port Arthur and the Battle of the Yellow Sea. Her large turrets formed the ship’s principal striking force. They are clearly visible at the ends of the hull in the museum’s plan, while the more numerous six-inch guns line the sides.

Behind that apparently simple arrangement lay magazines, hoists and hydraulic machinery. A barrel could not fight without its mounting and crew. Comparing Russian and Japanese armament by shell weight alone is therefore insufficient: the ship had to find the target, transmit data, supply ammunition and keep all these systems working under fire.

sections.title: Type 41: a name from a later period
paragraphs: The war also exposed the danger of heavy guns being damaged when a shell exploded prematurely in the bore. Such incidents are recorded for the Elswick family during the Russo-Japanese War. They are a reminder that the outcome depended on the combination of gun and ammunition, not the superiority of a calibre alone.

The designation “41st Year Type” was adopted on 25 December 1908, referring to the forty-first year of Emperor Meiji’s reign. On Mikasa herself, the twelve-inch/40 guns were replaced by more powerful twelve-inch/45 weapons during post-war reconstruction. That is a later chapter. A present-day museum caption, a later Japanese designation and the ship’s armament in 1904 need to be read separately, or a single battleship quietly acquires guns from several different periods.

name: Japanese 28-cm siege howitzer
summary: A heavy Osaka Arsenal howitzer originally designed for coastal defence and brought to Port Arthur. In 1904 it became one of the most prominent weapons used to bombard the fortifications and ships in the inner harbour.
intro: The gun most often associated with the siege of Port Arthur was originally intended to protect Japan’s coasts. Its short, thick barrel looks quite different from the long naval guns. A shell weighing approximately two hundred and twenty kilograms helps explain why moving this coastal weapon inland was such a significant development.

sections.title: From a coastal fortress to a besieged one
paragraphs: Japan’s 28-cm howitzer emerged from Osaka Artillery Arsenal’s work adapting European models. Researcher Yasufumi Kunimoto links its origins to an Italian design and the work of foreign specialists, dating completion of development and formal adoption to 1892. Reference books give other dates for individual stages. Development extended from the 1880s into the early 1890s.

A Japanese War Ministry file for October 1896 already contains an order for Osaka Arsenal to manufacture and deliver a 28-cm howitzer. It is a small but useful document, showing the weapon’s ordinary production history well before the famous siege. The gun was not invented specifically for Port Arthur.

sections.title: Weight that shaped its service
paragraphs: A calibre of 28 cm means a bore diameter of about 280 mm. This was a howitzer: a relatively short barrel and steep trajectory distinguished it from long naval guns intended for high muzzle velocity. In siege warfare this allowed targets behind obstacles to be attacked, though the capability did not guarantee a hit or destruction.

An American account of the siege gives a shell weight of 220 kg. It counts the barrel, carriage and metal platform separately: together they weighed far more than the gun alone. Moving a coastal weapon required transport and engineering work. Being placed near the infantry did not turn it into ordinary field artillery.

sections.title: Why the howitzers came to Port Arthur
paragraphs: According to Japanese military historian Hisayuki Yokoyama, after the unsuccessful general assault in August 1904 howitzers were brought to the siege from coastal fortresses, including the Tokyo Bay area. The artillery originally available had not provided enough firepower to take the Russian defences quickly. The heavy weapons were intended to change that, but did not remove the siege’s difficulties by themselves.

The howitzers fired at fortifications and ships in the inner harbour. The American report also mentions shelling of Vysokaya, or 203-Metre Hill. A Japanese archive preserves a photograph of a 28-cm howitzer’s trial firing near Wangjiadian, published in the Third Army’s album in April 1905. Behind the familiar image of the “siege gun” lay individual batteries and lengthy preparations.

sections.title: Not every shell, not a single cause
paragraphs: The American report notes unexploded 28-cm shells and distinguishes ordinary cast-iron from high-explosive ammunition. The familiar notion that every heavy shell necessarily contained a huge charge of Shimose, Japan’s picric-acid-based explosive, and inevitably destroyed everything around it cannot describe all the firing. Ammunition type mattered as much as the impressive diameter.

The system’s history continued after Port Arthur. An American survey of Japanese coastal artillery compiled in February 1946 gave it a separate section: substantial numbers of these old howitzers remained in Japanese fortifications. New models and longer ranges had appeared over the intervening decades, but the old heavy guns still occupied their positions. Their fame at Port Arthur far outshone the everyday service that followed.

name: Battleship Tsesarevich
summary: A French-built Russian battleship and Rear Admiral Vitgeft’s flagship at the Battle of the Yellow Sea. After internment at Qingdao she returned to the Baltic; in 1917 she was renamed Grazhdanin.
intro: At the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August) 1904, Tsesarevich remained afloat and retained most of her artillery, but lost steering control. Damage to one ship became a disaster for the whole column: the squadron commander, Wilgelm Vitgeft, and his staff were aboard. The flagship’s story shows why a strong hull and the ability to continue fighting were two different things.

sections.title: A French design for the Russian fleet
paragraphs: The French order was part of the effort to strengthen the fleet in the Far East. In 1898 a contract was signed with Forges et Chantiers de la Méditerranée, which built the ship at La Seyne, near Toulon. The design was the work of the engineer Amable Lagane. Construction began in 1899, she was launched in 1901 and commissioned in 1903. Her captain, Ivan Konstantinovich Grigorovich, spent several years supervising the work in France.

The French influence was immediately apparent: the high sides curved markedly inwards, and the secondary guns were mounted in turrets. Her Russian 305-mm guns were nevertheless products of the Obukhov Works. The Naval Ministry took sufficient interest in the design to use it as the starting point for the Borodino-class battleships, built in Russia.

sections.title: Twelve guns in six turrets
paragraphs: The four 305-mm guns were paired in the forward and after turrets. All twelve 152-mm Canet guns were also turret-mounted, in six twin installations. This protected the crews and machinery, but depended on working ammunition hoists, electric drives and communications. In addition to these two calibres, the battleship carried small guns against torpedo boats and torpedo tubes.

Two armour belts protected the sides, while a longitudinal torpedo bulkhead ran inside the hull: this additional wall was intended to limit flooding after an underwater explosion. Such protection did not make the ship invulnerable. On the first night of the war, however, its purpose became very practical: Tsesarevich took a torpedo hit aft and remained afloat.

sections.title: The war began with repairs
paragraphs: The battleship reached Port Arthur late in 1903. On the night preceding 27 January (9 February) 1904, Japanese torpedo boats attacked the Russian ships in the outer roadstead. The damaged Tsesarevich had to spend a long period out of the battle line. The base lacked a suitably large dry dock, so repairs used a caisson: a watertight enclosure fixed outside the hull around the hole and pumped dry.

In spring Grigorovich became commander of the port, and Nikolai Mikhailovich Ivanov took over the ship. After Stepan Makarov’s death, Tsesarevich became Rear Admiral Vitgeft’s flagship. By the July attempt to break through to Vladivostok, the repaired battleship was again leading the column. Months of work in a besieged harbour separated her first torpedo hit from the main battle of her war.

sections.title: A blow to the squadron’s command
paragraphs: In the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August), the ship received about twenty hits. The decisive shells struck around the bridges and conning tower. Vitgeft was killed on the open bridge. His chief of staff, Nikolai Matusevich, and Captain Ivanov were wounded. Damage to the steering and means of transmitting orders sent the flagship into an uncontrolled turn, disrupting the formation of the ships following her.

The damage report also lists wrecked compartments, broken wires and damaged instruments. “Control” depended on a whole network of people and mechanisms. Guns could still fire and engines could still run, but directing the ship effectively was becoming increasingly difficult. After the Russian column broke up, Tsesarevich neither returned to Port Arthur nor reached Vladivostok. She headed for the German base at Qingdao on the Chinese coast.

sections.title: A German port, then a different task
paragraphs: At Qingdao the German authorities required the battleship to disarm and interned her for the rest of the war: a neutral base could not serve as a permanent refuge and repair station for the Russian flagship. She did not surrender to the Japanese fleet. After the war the surviving ship returned to the Baltic and took part in training cruises.

In December 1908 Tsesarevich was once again a flagship, this time of Rear Admiral Vladimir Litvinov’s midshipmen’s training squadron. After the Messina earthquake, Russian sailors cleared rubble, gave assistance and carried survivors to safety. Several crews shared this work, so the number rescued by the entire squadron cannot be credited to one battleship. A Tsesarevich flag associated with the operation is preserved in the Central Naval Museum.

sections.title: From Tsesarevich to Grazhdanin
paragraphs: During the First World War the ship served in the Baltic. After the February Revolution of 1917, her monarchical name was replaced with Grazhdanin, meaning “Citizen”. Under that name the old battleship took part in the Moonsund operation, defending islands and straits off the coast of present-day Estonia. This was the same French-built hull that had survived Port Arthur, rather than a new ship with a revolutionary name.

After the war she was withdrawn from active service. She was broken up in the 1920s and struck from the navy list in 1925. The photograph of the damaged flagship at Qingdao therefore captures only the middle of her career. The return home, rescue work in Italy and another war on another sea still lay ahead.

name: Battleship Peresvet
summary: A battleship with a 254-mm main battery and Rear Admiral P. P. Ukhtomsky’s flagship during the defence of Port Arthur. Raised by Japan, she served as Sagami, was bought back by Russia in 1916 and sank off Port Said on her way north.
intro: Peresvet twice returned to service after serious damage and changed flags before regaining her Russian name. The defence of Port Arthur in 1904 was not the end of her story. Its final chapter unfolded at the entrance to the Suez Canal in January 1917; for the surviving sailors it continued in the camps and ports of Russia’s allies.

sections.title: A battleship for distant seas
paragraphs: Peresvet was built at the Baltic Works in St Petersburg: laid down in 1895, launched in 1898 and completed in 1901. The Naval Ministry wanted to combine a squadron battleship’s qualities with the capacity for long-range independent operations. Hence her high freeboard, large coal capacity and a main battery lighter than that of most contemporary battle-line opponents: 254 rather than 305 mm.

This concept should not be recast in the language of the later battlecruiser. Peresvet belonged to her own period and was intended to operate in a battleship squadron. Three steam engines drove three propellers, supplied by Belleville boilers. A designed speed of 18 knots and generous bunkers promised a wide cruising range, but overloading, the condition of the machinery and conditions at sea altered what could actually be achieved.

sections.title: What a lighter main battery meant
paragraphs: Four 254-mm guns were mounted in two turrets, a pair forward and a pair aft. They were supplemented by eleven 152-mm Canet guns in casemates, armoured compartments, and numerous smaller guns. The original outfit also included torpedo tubes. Comparing Peresvet with Tsesarevich or Poltava requires consideration of the whole arrangement, not a single calibre figure.

The armour belt protected the most important part of the hull, with unequal protection along its length. Coal and other loads affected how much of the belt stood above water. This was a genuine limitation of the design, but could not predetermine the outcome of every engagement. At Port Arthur the ship survived a fleet action and was lost later, at anchor under fire from heavy siege guns.

sections.title: Ukhtomsky’s flag, Boisman’s crew
paragraphs: Peresvet left for the Far East in autumn 1901 and reached Port Arthur in 1902. At the outbreak of war her captain was Vasily Arsenyevich Boisman. The squadron’s junior flag officer, Rear Admiral Pavel Petrovich Ukhtomsky, flew his flag aboard. These were distinct duties: the admiral directed the ships under his orders, while the captain was responsible for his own battleship and crew.

Peresvet escaped the opening night attack without a torpedo hit. Then came the sorties, alarms, repairs and transfers of men to the land front familiar to the besieged squadron. The ship’s gunnery officer, Vasily Nilovich Cherkasov, kept detailed records of the defence. Such accounts show the war from inside the ship, with its daily administration, allocation of ammunition and unceasing work by the crew.

sections.title: Returning from the Yellow Sea
paragraphs: In the action of 28 July (10 August) 1904, Peresvet received numerous hits. Boisman was badly wounded, and the executive officer, Apollon Apollonovich Dmitriyev, took command. The wounded captain survived the fortress’s surrender but died in Japanese captivity in 1905. His remains were brought back for burial in Vladivostok in 1906; these two dates are sometimes confused.

After Vitgeft’s death, Ukhtomsky had to re-establish command of the squadron. Damage to Peresvet’s masts and spars made signalling difficult, and the formation had already broken up. The battleship returned to Port Arthur with other ships. The attempted passage to Vladivostok had failed. Damaged upperworks and guns were repaired, but the base’s situation was worsening: the siege increasingly tied naval service to the defence of positions ashore.

sections.title: Raised and rebuilt
paragraphs: After the Japanese took 203-Metre Hill, they could more readily observe and correct their fire into the harbour. On 24 November (7 December) 1904, Peresvet came under heavy bombardment. Sea connections were opened to sink the damaged ship, and she settled on the bottom. The shallow harbour ended her career as a Russian fighting unit while leaving open the possibility of raising her.

The Japanese raised Peresvet in 1905 and renamed her Sagami. After a lengthy refit she served as a coast-defence ship. Repairs brought changes to equipment and armament, so Japanese specifications cannot be substituted for those of the Russian battleship in 1904. In 1916 Russia, now Japan’s ally, bought her back along with the former Poltava and Varyag. Peresvet regained her name, but under the new classification was called an armoured cruiser.

sections.title: She never reached the north
paragraphs: An accident delayed the new voyage: in May 1916 Peresvet grounded on rocks near Vladivostok. After being refloated and repaired, she headed west to join the forces Russia was assembling in the north. But on 22 December 1916 (4 January 1917), underwater explosions sank her off Port Said. Naval accounts link the disaster to a German minefield; the first reports also discussed a torpedo attack, while some of the crew demanded an investigation.

Rescue did not mean an early return home. The documents published by Belyakov describe the sailors’ stay at Port Said and their subsequent transfer to France. In summer 1917 the ship’s committee complained about supplies and the prolonged separation from Russia. The ship would not return a second time from a foreign navy; her men continued their own story after her loss.

name: Battleship Pobeda
summary: The last Peresvet-class battleship, which joined the Port Arthur squadron in 1903. After sinking, salvage and reconstruction she served in Japan as Suō, also spelt Suwo; unlike Peresvet, she never returned to Russia.
intro: On the day Petropavlovsk sank, another Russian battleship struck a Japanese mine. Pobeda suffered a large underwater hole but returned to harbour under her own power. Repairs, the Battle of the Yellow Sea and the bombardment of the base still lay ahead, followed by service under the Japanese flag.

sections.title: The third ship, a revised design
paragraphs: Pobeda was the third Peresvet-class ship. The Baltic Works began construction in 1898; she was officially laid down in 1899 and launched in 1900. By 1902 the battleship was already making voyages, although finishing work continued. She reached Port Arthur in June 1903, shortly before the war. It would be a mistake to regard her as an identical copy of Peresvet: the design changed during construction.

The broad concept remained the same: high freeboard, three engines and three propellers, substantial coal capacity and four 254-mm guns. Pobeda received strengthened main-battery mountings and more modern armour. These improvements matter in understanding the individual ship, but neither a trial speed nor the thickness of a particular plate can provide a complete answer about her fighting value.

sections.title: Heavy guns and the land front
paragraphs: The main battery comprised four 254-mm guns with barrels 45 calibres long, mounted in two twin turrets. The secondary battery originally numbered eleven 152-mm Canet guns; small quick-firing guns and torpedo tubes were also carried. As the siege progressed, some guns and ammunition went to the land defences, so the original inventory does not automatically describe every day of 1904.

sections.title: A mine after the flagship’s loss
paragraphs: At the outbreak of war Pobeda was commanded by Vasily Maximovich Zatsarenny. She escaped the opening night’s torpedoes and took part in the daylight action with the rest of the squadron. Her most dangerous early experience came on 31 March (13 April) 1904. Makarov’s flagship Petropavlovsk sank in the minefield off the base. Shortly afterwards Pobeda also struck a mine.

Water entered the hull and the ship listed, but internal bulkheads confined flooding to a limited part of the vessel. She returned to harbour under her own power. Repairs again required a caisson, a watertight enclosure attached outside the damaged hull, allowing work without a suitable dry dock. They kept the ship out of action for weeks, but did not end her part in the campaign.

sections.title: Damage described in detail
paragraphs: On 28 July (10 August) Pobeda sailed with the squadron for the attempt to reach Vladivostok. She took fewer hits than Peresvet, but this relative good fortune did not mean that she escaped serious damage. The report compiled after the action describes the specific effects of a shell: an armour plate shifted along one section of the side, fastenings were damaged and water entered the coal bunkers.

Other damage affected gun ports and equipment. Such records explain more than the bare statement that “the armour held”: protection could prevent a shell passing straight inside yet still leave the crew fighting flooding. After Vitgeft’s death and the break-up of the formation, Pobeda returned to Port Arthur. Repairing battle damage remained possible; restoring the squadron’s freedom of action was becoming much harder.

sections.title: From Port Arthur’s harbour to Qingdao
paragraphs: In autumn the ship became ever more closely involved in the fortress’s defence. Her men fought ashore while she remained a target for siege artillery. On 24 November (7 December) 1904, heavy Japanese shells caused underwater holes and flooding. Pobeda settled on the harbour bottom and ceased to be an operational Russian battleship.

After the fortress fell, the Japanese raised the ship and named her Suō, often rendered Suwo in older Russian literature. Following repairs she entered Japanese service in 1908 as a coast-defence ship. In 1914 the former Pobeda took part in the bombardment of German positions at Qingdao. In ten years both her flag and her enemy had changed: Russia and Japan were now fighting on the same side.

sections.title: How Suō’s service ended
paragraphs: In 1916 Russia bought back Peresvet, Poltava and Varyag from Japan. Pobeda was not among them: Suō continued in Japanese service, including gunnery training. She was disarmed in April 1922. That ended her career as an operational fighting ship.

The hull’s subsequent fate is less clear. Belov describes her capsizing during armour removal in July 1922 and gives two versions: breaking up that year, or righting the hull and using it as a hulk, an unpowered service vessel, until 1945–1946. Navypedia gives 1946 as the year of scrapping. A late date for the hull’s survival should therefore not be turned into an account of a battleship supposedly remaining in commission for another quarter-century.

name: Battleship Poltava
summary: A battleship of the Port Arthur squadron, sunk by siege artillery in the harbour. Raised by Japan, she served as Tango; bought back by Russia in 1916, she became Chesma and reached the Arctic Ocean.
intro: This ship bore the Russian name Poltava only during the first part of her career. After the defence of Port Arthur in 1904 she became the Japanese Tango, returned to Russia in 1916 and reached the north as Chesma. A new dreadnought had meanwhile taken her original name. The two Poltavas belonged to different generations of the fleet, rather than being a single renamed ship.

sections.title: Three ships of one generation
paragraphs: Poltava, Petropavlovsk and Sevastopol were built under the same programme of the early 1890s. Poltava was laid down in St Petersburg in 1892 and launched in 1894; construction and finishing work took several more years. When she reached Port Arthur in 1901 she was still a relatively new ship, although rapid naval development was already producing larger and faster designs.

The class is readily recognised by its two main-battery turrets, two funnels and four secondary turrets along the sides. Kinship did not mean identical equipment: the ships received different engines, boilers and armour. Poltava’s main belt used Krupp armour. One ship’s specifications therefore cannot be attributed to the other two without checking.

sections.title: Heavy guns and the demands of speed
paragraphs: Four Obukhov 305-mm guns, with barrels 40 calibres long, were mounted in two twin turrets. Of the twelve 152-mm Canet guns, eight were in four turrets and another four in a broadside battery. Unlike Tsesarevich, she did not have turret protection for the entire secondary battery. Smaller guns were intended chiefly to fight torpedo boats.

Two steam engines and fourteen cylindrical boilers drove two propellers. On trials she reached approximately sixteen and a half knots. In battle, however, what mattered was not the best measured-mile run but the ability to sustain speed with the column. Here Poltava’s service in the Yellow Sea exposed an unwelcome limitation: engine troubles and delays left her trailing and forced her to catch up with the squadron under fire.

sections.title: The men at the rear of the column
paragraphs: During the Russo-Japanese War the ship was commanded by Ivan Petrovich Uspensky, with Sergei Ivanovich Lutonin as executive officer. Their service involved more than the great July action. Poltava avoided torpedo damage on the war’s first night and took part in the daylight engagement of 27 January (9 February) 1904. Squadron sorties, watches and gunnery support for the defence followed.

At the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August), Poltava was last in the Russian line. When speed fell, the rear of the column was particularly exposed: the enemy could concentrate fire on the straggler. Yet the battleship could still return fire and close up with her own ships. Describing this as one Russian ship fighting the entire Japanese fleet independently would obscure the actual circumstances of the fleet action.

sections.title: The ship’s end in a shallow harbour
paragraphs: After the unsuccessful breakout, Poltava returned to Port Arthur. The damage report lists hits and affected parts of the ship; the very possibility of compiling it and beginning repairs distinguished the July battle from her later loss at anchor. In autumn Japanese siege guns increasingly struck the ships in harbour. Battleships built to move and manoeuvre lay in a confined base under plunging fire.

On 22 November (5 December) 1904, a heavy shell hit near Poltava’s after magazine for 47-mm ammunition. Fire spread towards adjacent propellant charges, followed by an explosion and extensive internal damage. The pumping vessel Silach helped extinguish the fire, but could not prevent the battleship sinking. The hull settled on the bottom. Surviving sailors continued to take part in the land defence.

sections.title: Returning under a different name
paragraphs: The Japanese raised Poltava in 1905, named her Tango and incorporated her into their fleet after repairs. Her hull outlasted the destruction of the Port Arthur squadron: relatively shallow water made it possible to return apparently lost ships to service. They were now prizes, however, with a different organisation aboard and altered equipment.

In 1916 Russia bought back the former Poltava, Peresvet and Varyag. The battleship could not regain her original name, because a dreadnought called Poltava was already serving in the Baltic. Renamed Chesma and classified as a battleship, she sailed west from Vladivostok with Varyag. Their route led through southern seas and the Suez Canal, with stops to load coal and finish repairs.

sections.title: North by way of the Mediterranean
paragraphs: The two ships parted company in the Mediterranean. Chesma joined the Allied fleet and took part in a demonstration of force against neutral Greece. Plans to use her in the Black Sea never resulted in a passage into that sea. After repairs in Britain, the battleship reached northern Russia early in 1917 and joined the Arctic Ocean forces.

The Civil War brought further changes: the ship came under British and then White control, serving as an unpowered vessel. In 1920 she passed to the Reds, but did not return to full fighting service. In the 1920s the old hull was sent for breaking up. A battleship that had sunk at Port Arthur in 1904 thus ended her existence thousands of miles from the scene of her first loss.
