name: Battleship Sevastopol
summary: A Poltava-class battleship that took part in the defence of Port Arthur. Under N. O. Essen she left the bombarded harbour for White Wolf Bay, endured night torpedo attacks and was scuttled in deep water before the fortress surrendered.
intro: Late in 1904, as heavy Japanese shells began destroying the ships in besieged Port Arthur’s harbour, Sevastopol was taken outside it. White Wolf Bay offered escape from that trap, but exposed her to night torpedo attacks. Her last weeks were spent fighting to remain afloat; they ended with deliberate scuttling away from the shallow harbour.

sections.title: One class, different machinery
paragraphs: Sevastopol was laid down in St Petersburg in 1892, launched in 1895 and completed around the turn of the century. She belonged to the same class as Poltava and Petropavlovsk: a relatively low hull, two funnels, two large turrets at the ends and four smaller ones along the sides. Her main fighting strength lay in four Obukhov 305-mm guns and twelve 152-mm Canet guns.

Eight secondary guns were in turrets and four in a broadside battery. Two engines drove two propellers, supplied by sixteen cylindrical boilers. Her sister Poltava had fourteen: even close relatives did not receive identical equipment. Machinery condition and crew training mattered as much in service as the design table. Before the war Sevastopol was repairing her engines and entered the conflict short of men.

sections.title: A captain from Novik
paragraphs: The battleship escaped the first torpedo attack on the outer roadstead, on the night preceding 27 January (9 February) 1904, without a hit. She suffered damage in the daylight action but remained operational. At the start of the campaign her captain was Nikolai Kuzmich Chernyshev. In March he was replaced by Nikolai Ottovich Essen, previously captain of the fast cruiser Novik.

His new ship was quite different: large, slower and with a propeller damaged in a collision with Peresvet. Once again repairs had to be carried out at a base without a suitably large dock. Sevastopol’s Port Arthur career was a succession of combat sorties and returns to repair damage. Each time, her continued service depended on specific work by the crew and port specialists.

sections.title: Three shots and a report
paragraphs: Essen’s report of 6 April describes in detail the gunfire four days earlier. Japanese ships were shelling the base from beyond Laoteshan; the Russians replied with indirect fire, shooting over the headland that hid their targets, using information passed by observers. Sevastopol fired three rounds from the forward 305-mm turret.

The third ended in a breakdown: recoil damaged the equipment that should have absorbed the gun’s movement and returned it to its firing position. Essen listed the broken parts and the warning immediately passed to Poltava. This small incident does not stand for the whole history of the ship’s artillery. It shows why a quoted maximum range did not guarantee trouble-free firing at every high angle of elevation.

sections.title: Mines, battle and further repairs
paragraphs: As the squadron returned from its June sortie, Sevastopol struck a mine. Flooding was contained, and a caisson, a watertight enclosure fitted outside the hole, allowed repairs that returned her to service. She was therefore able to fight in the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August), and returned to Port Arthur after the unsuccessful breakout.

The battle report records damage to bridges, communications, boats and ammunition-handling machinery. One fault was repaired during the action itself: a mechanical failure did not always put a gun permanently out of use. Later, in August, the battleship struck another mine after operating off the coast. More repairs followed. The ship survived into the final stage of the siege, but the squadron no longer had an undamaged reserve to draw upon.

sections.title: A bay instead of the bombarded harbour
paragraphs: After 203-Metre Hill fell, the Japanese could more easily observe and correct heavy-howitzer fire against the ships in harbour. Sevastopol escaped the fate of Poltava, Peresvet and Pobeda: on the night preceding 26 November (9 December), she was moved to White Wolf Bay. The museum record of a surviving photograph explicitly associates it with this sortie.

The new anchorage was not safe. Torpedo nets, floating barriers and gunfire from supporting ships and shore positions protected the battleship. Japanese torpedo boats attacked on several successive nights. Nets stopped some torpedoes; other explosions caused damage. The crew fought flooding, but damage aft and to the steering increasingly restricted independent movement. Leaving the harbour prolonged resistance without opening a way to freedom at sea.

sections.title: Silach’s final tow
paragraphs: By the time the fortress surrendered, the battleship remained afloat, but could no longer be saved for further operations. On 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905), the pumping vessel Silach towed Sevastopol into deep water. The men still aboard opened the hull to flood her and left the ship. The battleship capsized and came to rest on the seabed at a depth of about fifty metres.

Depth made the decisive difference from the ships resting inside the harbour: the Japanese did not raise her, and this hull had no new name or second career. The later Baltic dreadnought Sevastopol, also known as Parizhskaya Kommuna, was a different vessel. There is no Japanese or Soviet chapter to follow the Port Arthur battleship’s final tow.

name: 120-mm/45 Canet Gun, Pattern 1892
summary: A French-designed quick-firing gun manufactured in Russia. Six formed Novik’s main battery; after the Russo-Japanese War the system continued in use aboard ships and in coastal positions.
intro: In the Port Arthur squadron of 1904, the little Novik’s main weapons were guns that a large battleship would have regarded as auxiliary. Six 120-mm Canet guns allowed the scout to support torpedo craft and bombard the coast. The calibre also explains the limits of her capabilities: meeting a cruiser armed with six-inch guns meant facing substantially heavier shells.

sections.title: A French quick-firer for the Russian Navy
paragraphs: In 1891 a Russian delegation was shown the 120-mm and 152-mm quick-firing guns of the engineer Gustave Canet. The Naval Ministry bought a licence, and the Obukhov Works began production in 1892. The French name aboard Russian ships therefore identified the system’s origins; the guns themselves were also manufactured in Russia.

An important feature was the fixed round: projectile and cartridge case containing the propellant formed a single unit. This reduced the number of separate loading operations. The high rate achieved at demonstrations appealed to sailors expecting to face small, fast-moving torpedo boats. But rate of fire also depended on ammunition supply and the men’s endurance.

sections.title: What weighed twenty kilograms
paragraphs: The calibre of 120 mm is the diameter of the bore; 45 calibres is its nominal relative length. Multiplication gives 5.4 m. The old Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopaedic Dictionary already lists it as a 120-mm Canet gun of 45 calibres; its comparative table gives a projectile weight of 20.5 kg.

The projectile weighed less than the complete round carried by the crew. The gun and breech mechanism alone weighed about three tonnes, with mounting, shield and foundation additional. Behind the brief entry “six 120-mm guns” lay deck space, equipment weight and the continuous work of supplying ammunition.

sections.title: A scout’s main battery
paragraphs: Novik reached Port Arthur in 1903 with six 120-mm guns. During the war the cruiser frequently operated off the coast, covered light forces and supported troops. Lieutenant Andrei Shter’s diary shows sorties alternating with bombardments of shore positions: the scout’s main battery also worked for the land front.

In August 1904, after breaking out from Port Arthur, the cruiser was scuttled off Korsakov Post. Sailors remaining on Sakhalin removed her armament. A. A. Alliluyev’s study describes this work in detail. The guns and men could still be needed for the island’s defence even though the ship was already underwater.

sections.title: One type, several careers
paragraphs: After the war, strengthened versions of the system and new shells appeared. The range quoted for the later heavy Pattern 1911 projectile refers to different conditions from those in a pre-war table. Naval and coastal mountings also differed: more space ashore allowed different arrangements for installation and crew protection.

The guns remained in use in the First World War and Civil War, then in Soviet coastal defences. A distinct history developed in Finland, where surviving 120-mm Canet guns received modified mountings. One was used for training until 1993 and is now on Kuivasaari. Its recoil mechanism above the barrel belongs to this Finnish history, made especially clear by the photograph.

name: 254-mm/45 Obukhov Gun
summary: The ten-inch system forming Peresvet’s and Pobeda’s main batteries. A shared designation conceals different versions: the early lightweight barrels and the strengthened guns had different ballistic characteristics.
intro: At Port Arthur in 1904, Peresvet and Pobeda each had four main guns, just like the other battleships beside them. Their shells, however, were considerably lighter than twelve-inch projectiles. The ships were designed to combine squadron and cruising duties, and the choice of a ten-inch calibre became a defining feature. It then emerged that the same calibre did not necessarily mean identical guns.

sections.title: A joint concept for army and navy
paragraphs: The system developed from the early 1890s as part of work on naval and coastal artillery. Reference books commonly call it “Pattern 1891”. Yet the naval and land versions differed in construction and weight; a single table heading did not make them fully interchangeable.

The Obukhov Works supplied guns for several classes of ship. Peresvet’s four barrels were paired in the forward and after turrets. Electric drives trained the mountings and powered ammunition handling. For the navy this was an important change from earlier hydraulic mechanisms.

sections.title: The price of saving weight
paragraphs: Trials of the early 254-mm guns revealed a tendency for cracks to develop in the bores. R. M. Melnikov describes muzzle velocity being reduced to about 695 m/s, followed by the strengthening of the guns. The saving in weight had brought limitations in strength; the system itself needed modification.

Pobeda received a heavier version with a higher muzzle velocity: a specialist summary gives about 777 m/s, against roughly 693 m/s for Peresvet. The few metres per second between the two estimates for the early variant reflect the precision of the sources. The difference between the ships’ versions is much more significant. Giving both the highest figure would erase the history of the modifications.

sections.title: A shell weighing two hundred and twenty-five kilograms
paragraphs: Ten inches is 254 mm. A relative length of 45 calibres corresponds to about 11.43 m under the nominal designation. The Russian-service projectile weighed about 225 kg. This was still heavy naval artillery, requiring magazines, hoists and many people working around the four visible barrels.

Projectile weight helps convey the scale, but cannot replace information about its construction and the circumstances of impact. Similarly, maximum range depended on the particular gun and turret version. Published accounts even disagree over Pobeda’s elevation angles; reducing such tables to one undisputed range for the entire type would be premature.

sections.title: What happened around the turret
paragraphs: In 1904 the ten-inch guns of both battleships served with the Port Arthur squadron, including the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 28 July (10 August). The notes of Peresvet’s senior gunnery officer, Vasily Cherkasov, show the turret within the workings of the ship: damaged drives, the transmission of orders and men at the machinery.

Hits on the forward turret disrupted its operation and killed men. Yet the ship stayed afloat and returned to harbour. Such incidents also belong to the story of a heavy gun: a barrel may survive while its mounting loses the ability to train normally or receive ammunition. Protection of people and machinery was part of the whole turret’s fighting value.

sections.title: The family’s long service
paragraphs: Late in 1904 Peresvet and Pobeda sank at Port Arthur; the Japanese raised and restored them as Sagami and Suwo. A Japanese photographic album published in 1906 shows the condition of the sunken Peresvet’s turret. This is the aftermath of the siege, not an undamaged mounting before the war.

The ten-inch system also survived aboard other Russian ships. A Naval Ministry return for 1917 lists ten guns, four of them aboard Rostislav. Related coastal guns served alongside them. Their later histories grew from the same development, but a museum coastal mounting does not show how a naval turret was arranged.

name: 47-mm Single-Barrelled Hotchkiss Gun
summary: A quick-firing single-barrelled gun widely used by the Russian Navy against torpedo boats. At Port Arthur its large numbers went hand in hand with the rapidly apparent limitations of its small projectile.
intro: In a photograph of a Port Arthur squadron battleship in 1904, it is easy to notice the main turrets and overlook the little guns on the bridges. There could be several dozen of them. Each meant men, ammunition and an assigned task: stopping a torpedo boat before it could launch. One of the commonest weapons for the job was the single-barrelled 47-mm Hotchkiss.

sections.title: One name, several systems
paragraphs: The French firm Hotchkiss et Cie manufactured several small-calibre systems. Single-barrelled weapons existed alongside five-barrelled revolving guns, in which several barrels formed a rotating cluster. Russian inventories include the designations 47/1 and 47/5. Here the figure after the slash is the number of barrels, not their length.

The single-barrelled system spread through the Russian Navy in the 1880s. Guns were purchased abroad and manufactured in Russia. The Central Naval Museum holds a naval 47-mm gun made by the Obukhov Works in 1892. It confirms that by the war of 1904 this was an established weapon, rather than a hurried innovation of the siege.

sections.title: A small gun on a large ship
paragraphs: The Russian single-barrelled gun had a barrel approximately 43.5 calibres long, or about two metres. Its projectile weighed around a kilogram and a half. The complete round, including case and propellant, was heavier. The gun and breech mechanism alone weighed about 235 kg; comparing museum examples requires the weight of the appropriate mounting to be added.

Manual handling and a relatively small round allowed a high rate of fire. The museum gives 15 rounds per minute, the specialist reference 20. These figures were not established under demonstrably identical conditions, so they cannot be promised throughout a battle. Sailors needed working mechanisms, a supply of ready rounds and the ability to see the target.

sections.title: Why the mounting matters
paragraphs: The first imported guns were fitted to rigid carriages without recoil mechanisms. Hydraulic mountings followed: an example was purchased from Hotchkiss in 1888, after which the Obukhov Works produced Russian versions. An identical caption of “47-mm Hotchkiss” therefore does not identify the particular mounting in front of us.

The photograph of a museum gun on wheels shows another possibility: transferring a naval weapon to a field carriage. This example illustrates that combination, but proves nothing by itself about a particular battery at Port Arthur. A deck pedestal and a wheeled carriage belonged to different service conditions.

sections.title: War tested the earlier assumptions
paragraphs: Novik’s original armament included six 47-mm Hotchkiss guns. On a large ship their role remained auxiliary. In a memorandum after the action of 28 July 1904, Peresvet’s gunnery officer Vasily Cherkasov judged 47-mm guns unsuitable for squadron combat, allowing them a limited role against torpedo attacks.

This was a participant’s assessment, not a claim that every such gun was invariably useless. Yet earlier hopes for small-calibre anti-torpedo-boat guns plainly needed reconsideration. A small shell and high rate of fire no longer seemed sufficient protection against growing torpedo craft. After the war, 47-mm guns began to be removed from large ships.

sections.title: From battleship decks to small craft
paragraphs: Removal from battleships did not mean the system disappeared. In the First World War and Civil War, single-barrelled Hotchkiss guns remained in service aboard light vessels and river flotilla craft. Even such a gun could substantially strengthen a small vessel, although its limitations against a large warship remained.

Some guns were adapted for use against aircraft; others eventually entered museum collections. The once-common naval quick-firer left several different forms behind: a naval gun on a pedestal, a wheeled field mounting and a later conversion. They become more interesting when both the shared system and the history of the individual exhibit are understood.

name: Cruiser Askold
summary: A fast German-built cruiser with five funnels, flagship of Port Arthur’s cruiser division. After the Battle of the Yellow Sea she escaped to Shanghai; later she fought in the Mediterranean and served in the Russian north.
intro: Five tall funnels made Askold one of the most recognisable ships of the Port Arthur squadron in 1904. But her story rests on more than a striking silhouette. The fast cruiser escaped a lost battle, was then immobilised by China’s neutrality, and in the next war travelled from the Pacific to the Dardanelles and Murmansk.

sections.title: An order placed in Kiel
paragraphs: Askold was ordered from the German firm Germania in 1898 to strengthen the fleet in the Far East. Work at Kiel began before the detailed drawings were finally approved. She was officially laid down in 1899 and launched in 1900; trials continued in 1901, while acceptance and the hoisting of the St Andrew’s flag were completed early in 1902.

Her first captain, Nikolai Karlovich Reitsenstein, supervised construction and chaired the acceptance commission. Russian specialists required checks on the long, narrow hull’s strength and reinforcement of certain structures. They also disputed the bow shape and bilge keels, underwater longitudinal fins that reduce rolling. High speed had to be reconciled with strength and behaviour in a seaway.

sections.title: Fast, but without an armour belt
paragraphs: Three steam engines drove three propellers, supplied by nineteen Schultz–Thornycroft boilers. On trials Askold comfortably exceeded the contracted 23 knots. A successful trial run did not mean the same speed at any load or in any machinery condition. Five funnels served the boiler installation; they were not in themselves a measure of fighting strength.

The ship was a protected cruiser: an armoured deck with slopes down towards the sides covered the principal machinery and magazines, but there was no continuous side belt. Twelve 152-mm Canet guns formed the main battery. They stood in open deck mountings behind shields, not in turrets. Numerous smaller guns were intended chiefly to repel torpedo boats.

sections.title: A scout’s everyday work
paragraphs: Askold arrived at Port Arthur in 1903. By the outbreak of war the ship was commanded by K. A. Grammatchikov; Reitzenstein commanded the cruiser division and flew his flag aboard Askold. The admiral and captain had different responsibilities: one directed the division, the other the individual ship.

The report on reconnaissance near the Blonde Islands on 5 February (18 February) 1904 explains the fast cruiser’s role. She first returned with Bayan after that ship suffered engine trouble, then put out again. Finding enemy cruisers and torpedo boats near the islands, Grammatchikov stopped closing, fearing that he would be cut off as darkness fell. Reconnaissance required bringing information home while preserving the ship, rather than turning every encounter into a fight. On the return after dark he initially maintained full speed and altered course, then reduced to ten knots to lessen smoke and sparks from the funnels. At night the ship’s own smoke trail could aid detection.

sections.title: Out of battle, then out of the war
paragraphs: On 28 July (10 August) 1904, Askold sailed with the squadron for the attempted breakout to Vladivostok. After Vitgeft’s death and the disorder in the Russian column, Reitzenstein led his cruisers on an independent attempt to leave the battle. The whole division did not escape together: Askold and Novik broke clear, while Diana and Pallada met different fates.

Damaged, Askold headed for Shanghai rather than Vladivostok. China remained neutral, and the cruiser could not use its port indefinitely to restore her fighting capacity and resume sorties. After diplomatic disputes she was disarmed and interned for the rest of the war. The breakout saved hull and crew from Port Arthur’s surrender, but did not return them to an active squadron.

sections.title: Another war on another coast
paragraphs: After the war Askold served in the Siberian Flotilla. At the start of the First World War she operated with the Allies on ocean routes, then moved to the Mediterranean. In 1915 her guns and boats helped support the French landing at Kum Kale during the Dardanelles campaign. The familiar guns were now firing against the Ottoman coast.

Hard service required extensive repairs at Toulon in 1916. An explosion in a magazine there was followed by arrests and the execution of four sailors. The monograph’s authors note the absence of direct evidence against the condemned men; those responsible for the explosion cannot be described as conclusively identified. The ship’s history includes this painful episode in relations within the crew as well as her combat operations.

sections.title: Glory IV and the final passage
paragraphs: In 1917 Askold reached Kola Bay and joined the Arctic Ocean forces. After the revolution and demobilisation, men were short and machinery needed work. British forces seized the cruiser in 1918; renamed Glory IV, she was used as a floating barracks, then taken to Britain.

In the early 1920s her return to Soviet Russia was discussed. A commission including the naval architect Alexei Krylov inspected the ship to decide whether repair was worthwhile. Restoration was considered too expensive. After arrangements for her transfer were settled, Askold was sold for breaking up in Germany in 1922. The five-funnelled ship had no further fighting career: her last voyage was to the breakers.

name: Cruiser Pallada
summary: A protected cruiser torpedoed on the first night of the war and later sunk in Port Arthur’s harbour. The Japanese raised her and commissioned her as Tsugaru; after training service and conversion to a minelayer, she became a target.
intro: Port Arthur’s Pallada had a second career under the Japanese flag. Disabled by a torpedo on the opening night of the war in 1904 and sunk by siege artillery at the end of that year, she was raised and restored. She must therefore be distinguished from the other Pallada, an armoured cruiser sunk in the Baltic in 1914.

sections.title: The lead ship of the Diana class
paragraphs: Pallada was built at Galerny Island in St Petersburg alongside Diana; Aurora, built at the New Admiralty, was the third ship. Officially laid down in 1897, Pallada was launched in 1899 and commissioned in 1901. The class became known by Diana’s name although Pallada was the lead ship. Even the designation of these three related vessels therefore needs a little explanation.

The design was intended for reconnaissance with the squadron and operations against maritime communications. It was created before German yards presented Russia with faster cruisers from the newer orders. By 1904 the difference was clear: Pallada, capable of roughly nineteen knots, was slower than Askold and Novik. Her whole career cannot be explained by speed alone, however; mine damage and the circumstances of the besieged base imposed other demands.

sections.title: Armour below deck, guns above
paragraphs: Three steam engines, three propellers and twenty-four Belleville boilers occupied much of the hull. A curved armoured deck covered magazines and machinery: the central part ran almost horizontally, while its edges sloped down towards the sides. There was no continuous side belt. Hence the term “protected cruiser”, distinguishing her from the later armoured Pallada.

Her principal armament was eight 152-mm Canet guns with barrels 45 calibres long. They were deck-mounted; smaller quick-firing guns and torpedo tubes were also carried. The artillery return described the original outfit, but during the siege guns and men went to positions ashore. The gun count at the start of service cannot automatically be applied to its final month.

sections.title: Searchlights on the outer roadstead
paragraphs: Pallada reached Port Arthur in 1903. Before the war Vladimir Simonovich Sarnavsky became her captain. On the evening of 26 January (8 February) 1904, the cruiser lay in the outer roadstead on illumination duty, sweeping the approaches to the Russian squadron with searchlights. These aided observation while also marking the ship’s position.

During the night attack a Japanese torpedo struck the port side near a coal bunker. Flooding and fire threatened the compartments behind it; the crew fought the flames and covered the hole with collision mats, sheets temporarily closing the opening from outside. Retvizan and Tsesarevich were also torpedoed. Stark reported that the less severely damaged Pallada remained near the shallows, letting the battleships enter the harbour first.

sections.title: Repairs and the return from the Yellow Sea
paragraphs: After repairs the cruiser rejoined the squadron’s operations. The crew’s war continued between the major actions: watches, sorties, work on the damaged hull and maintaining the guns were part of daily service. The first torpedo did not determine Pallada’s final fate, although it deprived the squadron of a cruiser early in the campaign.

On 28 July (10 August), she sailed with the main force to break through to Vladivostok. After Vitgeft’s death the Russian column fell into disorder. Askold and Novik’s escape from the action did not take the whole cruiser division with them. Pallada returned to Port Arthur with the battleships. She had survived the naval battle but was again in a base approached ever more closely by Japanese troops.

sections.title: A ship under fire from land
paragraphs: In autumn much of the artillery and many sailors served the fortress’s defences. Ships remaining in harbour suffered increasingly from siege fire. Taking 203-Metre Hill gave the Japanese a convenient observation point from which to correct their fire against the inner roadstead. The ships’ own protective decks could not shelter them from the steep trajectories of heavy shells.

On 24 November (7 December) 1904, several hits exhausted Pallada’s reserve buoyancy, and she settled on the harbour bottom. Her crew could no longer return her to the line. Yet this manner of sinking left the hull accessible for salvage: after the fortress fell, Japanese specialists could survey the vessel and arrange reconstruction. Russian fighting service ended, while the ship herself continued to exist.

sections.title: Training ship, minelayer and target
paragraphs: In 1905 the Japanese raised Pallada and renamed her Tsugaru. Following lengthy repairs at Sasebo, she was used to train sailors. New equipment and the Japanese armament belong to that period, rather than to the Russian cruiser on the war’s first night. In 1920 Tsugaru was converted to a minelayer, with deck rails fitted for embarking and laying mines.

Two years later she was removed from the fleet. Her hull became a target and was sunk during an aviation exercise in 1924. That was the end of Port Arthur’s Pallada. The story of her loss to a German submarine in 1914 belongs to a different, newer cruiser. The two ships shared a name, but differed in design, theatre of service and final date.

name: Cruiser Diana
summary: A protected cruiser of the Port Arthur squadron that sailed to French Saigon after the Battle of the Yellow Sea. She returned to the Baltic, served in the First World War and was broken up in the 1920s; her sister Aurora was a separate ship.
intro: In 1904 the damaged Diana travelled from the Yellow Sea to Saigon, much farther than the distance to Vladivostok, the squadron’s intended destination. This seems odd until coal consumption, the need to keep boilers ready for a chase and an underwater hole are considered. Captain Alexander Lieven’s decision saved the ship but took her out of the war.

sections.title: Sister to Pallada and Aurora
paragraphs: Diana was built at Galerny Island in St Petersburg. Officially laid down in 1897, she was launched in 1899 and commissioned in 1901. Pallada and Aurora were built to the same design. The designation “Diana class” became established for all three, although Pallada was regarded as the lead ship. Three similar silhouettes meant three separate crews and three different fates.

The design was intended for reconnaissance with the squadron and operations against enemy shipping. While the ships were being completed, Russia received faster cruisers ordered abroad. By the outbreak of war Diana was already slower than the new scouts. Her long career later required rebuilding and rearmament; the original design table cannot describe the ship for every subsequent year.

sections.title: What the armoured deck protected
paragraphs: The cruiser had three steam engines, three propellers and twenty-four Belleville boilers. An armoured deck covered the principal machinery and magazines from above, its edges sloping down towards the sides. There was no side armour belt. This explains the term “protected cruiser” and its limits: upper compartments, deck-gun crews and some equipment remained much more vulnerable.

Diana originally carried eight 152-mm Canet guns. By the July action in 1904, two had been transferred to Retvizan, together with four 75-mm guns. Lieven’s report lists the shortage immediately before departure. The six remaining 152-mm guns are an important correction to the usual reference figure of eight when discussing the Battle of the Yellow Sea itself.

sections.title: Months at a besieged base
paragraphs: In 1902 Diana sailed to the Far East with Rear Admiral Ewald Stackelberg’s squadron, reaching Port Arthur in 1903. She escaped the opening night’s torpedo attack without a hit, unlike her sister Pallada. She then served with the squadron off the besieged base. Apparently uneventful harbour life included combat readiness, sorties and preparations for another attempt to break out.

Alexander Alexandrovich Lieven took command in May 1904. His executive officer was Vladimir Ivanovich Semyonov, who later described the war in Rasplata, or The Reckoning. Their accounts do not speak for every participant, but show practical calculations aboard. Before the July departure, for example, loading the last coal dragged on until morning because it was awkward to unload from the transport Angara.

sections.title: A hole below water and a scattered division
paragraphs: On 28 July (10 August) 1904, Diana sailed with the squadron for Vladivostok. After Vitgeft’s death and the disorder in the formation, Lieven did not follow the battleships back to Port Arthur. The cruiser headed south. She could not keep up with the faster Askold and Novik; for a time the destroyer Grozovoy accompanied her.

Diana’s most serious damage was an underwater hole. The crew shored it up from inside, but could no longer freely choose speed and course. A decision was needed on whether a roundabout passage to Vladivostok remained possible. A large coal balance on paper did not equal fuel immediately available for the furnaces: some was in reserve bunkers and had to be shifted by hard manual work.

sections.title: Why Saigon proved more reachable
paragraphs: Economical speed gave a comparatively long range. In the Yellow Sea, however, boilers had to be ready to accelerate on meeting the enemy, increasing consumption. The officers weighed fuel reserves, the damaged hull’s condition and the possibility of repairs in a neutral port. A call at Qingdao threatened rapid internment; they decided to head south for French possessions.

Via Guangzhouwan and Haiphong the cruiser reached Saigon, now Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam. They hoped to repair the damage and resume service. Permission was delayed, however, and the French authorities eventually required disarmament. Diana remained interned until the war ended. The long distance travelled does not disprove Lieven’s calculations: a safe, economical passage and a breakout through waters held by the enemy fleet required different fuel expenditure and machinery readiness.

sections.title: Different guns, a different ending
paragraphs: Early in 1906 Diana returned to the Baltic. After repairs she undertook training service. During the First World War she was rearmed: installation and familiarisation with ten 130-mm guns in place of the former main battery were completed in summer 1915. In 1916 she fought German torpedo craft alongside Gromoboi. This was no longer the Diana with six 152-mm guns of the July breakout.

After the revolution the ship was withdrawn from active service and laid up. In 1922 the worn-out hull was sold for breaking up and towed to Germany after useful equipment had been removed. Aurora was considered suitable for restoration as a training ship. Diana did not become a memorial: her history ended at the breakers, although she had survived both Port Arthur and the next war.

name: Cruiser Boyarin
summary: A small Danish-built scout cruiser that reached Port Arthur in 1903. Early in the war she struck a Russian minefield off Dalny, was abandoned by her crew and sank several days later.
intro: In February 1904 Boyarin sailed towards Dalny to search for enemy torpedo boats after news of the minelayer Yenisei’s loss. Instead of fighting the Japanese, she herself struck a Russian mine. The cruiser was abandoned while still afloat; a later salvage attempt could not save her for the fleet. Time elapsed between the explosion and the final loss, a distinction easily lost in a short account.

sections.title: The Danish order
paragraphs: Boyarin was built at Burmeister & Wain in Copenhagen. The Danish firm’s proposal arrived in 1898, when the Russian Navy had already selected the German Novik as a model for a small, fast scout. The Naval Technical Committee nevertheless examined another design. Displacement, engine power, protection and speed requirements changed during negotiations.

A contract was signed in 1899, construction got underway in 1900, she was launched in 1901 and trials followed in 1902. The initial concept for a small vessel grew to a design displacement of 3200 tonnes. Bilge keels, underwater fins reducing rolling, were fitted; a slight reduction in contracted speed was accepted for their sake. This was an independent Danish design, not another hull built exactly to Novik’s drawings.

sections.title: A small scout with six guns
paragraphs: Three funnels, two masts and small raised decks forward and aft distinguished Boyarin from the narrower, three-shaft Novik. Two steam engines drove two propellers, supplied by sixteen Belleville boilers. In a six-hour trial the cruiser made 22.6 knots, exceeding the revised contractual requirement of 21.75 knots.

Her main armament was six 120-mm Canet guns with barrels 45 calibres long, supplemented by small guns, a landing gun and five torpedo tubes. A sloping armoured deck protected the machinery and magazines from above; there was no continuous side belt. The ship was intended for reconnaissance, communications and operations with torpedo craft. Serving alongside a battleship squadron did not give her its protection or purpose.

sections.title: Less than a year at Port Arthur
paragraphs: In autumn 1902 Captain Vladimir Fyodorovich Sarychev took Boyarin from Kronstadt towards the Far East. She reached Port Arthur in May 1903. Squadron commander Oskar Stark approved of the new ship’s strength, seakeeping and coal consumption. His assessment concerned practical service, not simply a comparison of top speeds.

Over the next few months the cruiser took part in manoeuvres and acted as a station ship, representing the Russian Navy in an assigned foreign port. Before the war that station was Chemulpo in Korea; after Varyag arrived, Boyarin rejoined the squadron. Her pre-war story thus involved passages between bases and Russia’s presence off Korea as well as the accident still to come.

sections.title: Orders to sail for Dalny
paragraphs: In the opening days of the Russo-Japanese War, Boyarin served as a scout. Meanwhile the minelayer Yenisei laid a field on the approaches to Dalny in Talienwan Bay. The Russians wanted to keep the enemy away from the port, but their own ships also needed accurate information about the new mines. On 29 January (11 February) 1904, Yenisei herself struck a mine and sank.

Reports of this disaster became mixed with the suggestion that Japanese torpedo boats had attacked. Boyarin was sent to the area. In his report Sarychev explained that he had orders to find and destroy enemy torpedo craft near Dalny. An explosion occurred by the port side as she approached the Sanshantao islands. The cruiser had entered the Russian minefield intended to protect this same stretch of coast.

sections.title: What the captain saw
paragraphs: Sarychev’s report describes the list, flooding and rapid loss of steam. He wrote that he feared a second explosion as the ship drifted towards the shore and minefield. The crew first tried to pump out water and apply a collision mat, a sheet temporarily covering the hole. Sarychev then ordered them to transfer to the approaching destroyers.

The crew took off logs, charts, money and secret documents; personal possessions remained. The sea valves were not opened to scuttle the ship: the captain expected her to sink or strike another mine. That was his own explanation of the decision. The fact remains that the abandoned Boyarin stayed afloat for some time. Abandonment and final loss were not a single moment.

sections.title: Salvage and the limits of blame
paragraphs: The cruiser was later inspected and considered still worth attempting to save. Worsening weather, drifting and further damage finally removed that possibility. By 31 January (13 February) 1904, Boyarin was lost. The Japanese did not acquire her as a restored prize; the hull had no further service or new name.

Sarychev faced a court over his actions. His report lets us examine what he feared and why he took the men off; it does not prove that every means of saving the ship had been exhausted. Yet the single label “abandoned” is insufficient too: understanding requires attention to the damage, loss of steam, movement among Russian mines and the subsequent salvage attempt. Boyarin’s brief service ended close to the Russian port she was meant to protect.

name: Battleship Hatsuse
summary: A British-built Japanese battleship of the Shikishima class. She sank off Port Arthur on 2 (15) May 1904 in the minefield laid by Amur; together with Yashima, she represented Japan’s greatest single loss of battleships during the war.
intro: On the morning of 2 (15) May 1904, Hatsuse was still the flagship of a three-battleship force off Port Arthur. Within hours she was gone. Her heavy guns and armour were intended for battle with the Russian squadron, but the final blow came from underwater. After the first explosion there was time to attempt a rescue; after the second, there was almost none.

sections.title: From Elswick to the Japanese battle line
paragraphs: Hatsuse was built in Britain at Armstrong’s Elswick yard on the River Tyne. Laid down in January 1898, she was launched on 27 June 1899 and completed on 18 January 1901. The order formed part of Japan’s naval expansion after its war with China. Japan was purchasing ships abroad to fight together in a battle line, rather than acquiring isolated showpieces.

Hatsuse belonged to the Shikishima class, a development of the British Majestic design. The contemporary naval writer Fred Jane discussed her alongside Asahi and Mikasa, while noting differences in appearance and construction. Hatsuse had three funnels; the other two had two apiece. Early in 1901, before sailing to join her fleet, the new battleship represented Japan at Queen Victoria’s funeral.

sections.title: Armour and machinery for fleet action
paragraphs: Normal displacement was about fifteen thousand tonnes. Two triple-expansion steam engines drove two propellers, with steam supplied by twenty-five Belleville boilers. Designed speed was about eighteen knots. During trials in December 1900, the average of four measured-mile runs reached 19.1 knots. A successful trial did not mean that the ship could always maintain that speed under any load.

An armoured belt protected the side, reaching its greatest thickness amidships: up to 229 mm. Behind it, the sloping sides of the armoured deck provided another barrier between incoming shells and the machinery. Protection depended on these barriers working together. The belt was primarily intended to resist shell hits near the waterline. An underwater explosion could damage quite different parts of the hull, disable steering and force the crew to fight flooding instead of firing their guns.

sections.title: Four heavy guns
paragraphs: The main battery comprised four Armstrong 12-inch guns—approximately 305 mm—with barrels forty calibres long. They were mounted in pairs in turrets forward and aft. Fourteen 152 mm guns supported the heavy battery, in casemates: armoured compartments along the sides, with openings for the guns. Smaller quick-firing guns were intended chiefly for use against torpedo boats.

The main guns belonged to the Elswick export family also carried by Mikasa. Jane explicitly traces Japan’s adoption of these weapons to Fuji and Yashima, then lists their successors. A common main calibre helped ships of different generations fight in one line; their armour, mountings and ability to withstand damage still differed. Hatsuse also carried torpedo tubes, though artillery remained her principal weapon.

sections.title: A flagship off the Russian base
paragraphs: At the outbreak of war, Captain Nakao Yū commanded the ship, while Rear Admiral Nashiba Tokioki flew his flag aboard her. The captain was responsible for the battleship; the admiral directed the force. Hatsuse took part in the daylight action off Port Arthur on 27 January (9 February) 1904. Her subsequent service centred on the blockade: watching the Russian squadron and restricting its freedom to put to sea.

Blockade duty meant returning to familiar stretches of water. The Russians exploited this routine. On 1 (14) May, the minelayer Amur laid a field across the Japanese ships’ route. The following day Hatsuse, Shikishima and Yashima approached Port Arthur with their accompanying vessels. Here the minelaying operation became part of the battleship’s own story, on the seaward approaches to the Russian base.

sections.title: Two explosions, little time to escape
paragraphs: The first mine damaged Hatsuse’s stern and steering. She remained afloat, and attempts were made to approach her to give assistance and take her in tow. Then she struck a second mine. Her ammunition exploded, and the battleship sank rapidly. Postwar accounts describe minutes, rather than hours of damage control. Hundreds of sailors died. Nakao Yū and Nashiba were among those rescued; an exact death toll cannot be calculated by subtracting an early estimate of survivors from the ship’s nominal complement.

Even nearby ships did not immediately understand what was happening. Historian Chiharu Inaba, studying Japanese records of the underwater threat, cites signals warning of possible Russian submarines. Yashima was also damaged. Those reports of an unseen attacker must be distinguished from the established cause: both battleships had struck Russian mines. No submarine attack is needed to explain the sudden explosions.

sections.title: A gap in the next battle line
paragraphs: Hatsuse was never raised or transferred to another navy. Her three years of service ended off Port Arthur; there was no later name or postwar modernisation. Photographs of the intact ship show a vessel already lost before the major battles that summer and beyond. She therefore had no place in Japan’s battle line at the Yellow Sea or Tsushima.

Japan also lost Yashima that day, though her sinking followed a different course. Of six modern Japanese battleships, four remained. This was a severe blow to the blockading force, but the blockade continued. Hatsuse’s story ends with a specific gap in the Japanese line—and with the survival of people who could still be picked up as a large warship went down.

name: Battleship Yashima
summary: One of Japan’s first modern battleships, built at Elswick under the same programme as Fuji. On 2 (15) May 1904 she struck Amur’s mines off Port Arthur and later sank after attempts to save her; news of the loss remained the subject of rumours for a long time.
intro: After the explosion off Port Arthur on 2 (15) May 1904, Yashima had something that the nearby Hatsuse scarcely did: time. There was still a chance to tow the battleship away, fight the flooding and take her people off. The ship herself could not be saved. Her final hours show why striking a mine, being abandoned by the crew and finally sinking are three separate events.

sections.title: Japan’s first generation of large battleships
paragraphs: Yashima and Fuji preceded Mikasa and Hatsuse. Japan needed seagoing battleships capable of fighting heavy warships in a battle line, but its own industry could not yet build such vessels independently. The orders went to Britain: Fuji to Thames Ironworks and Yashima to Armstrong’s Elswick yard. Related designs did not mean that the two hulls were built on the same slipway.

Construction of Yashima began in 1894. She was launched on 28 February 1896 and completed on 9 September 1897. Jane describes the design as a development of the British Royal Sovereign class. The smaller Japanese ship carried 12-inch guns instead of the larger British weapons, and Harvey steel armour. Her name referred to Japan itself: Yashima was one of the country’s traditional names. By the war of 1904, the battleship had already served under the Japanese flag for several years.

sections.title: Two speeds for one ship
paragraphs: Official trials took place near the mouth of the Tyne on 13 and 14 July 1897. The report by engineer S. Sasow gives an average of 19.227 knots for four runs under forced draught. The following day, a six-hour natural-draught trial produced 17.35 knots at lower power. Forced draught meant supplying additional air to the furnaces. Two different speeds in the records therefore need not be contradictory: the boilers were working under different conditions.

This distinction tells us more than a single impressive record. Two triple-expansion engines drove two propellers; coal, steam, machinery condition and operating regime determined the available speed. The same report measured turning performance: how tight a circle the ship described when the helm was put over. Trials assessed the handling of a large battleship as well as her speed. Neither 19.227 knots nor a small turning circle guaranteed escape from damage.

sections.title: A thick belt and exposed guns
paragraphs: Four Armstrong 305 mm guns with barrels forty calibres long stood in pairs in the forward and after mountings. Ten 152 mm guns formed the secondary battery. Some had casemate protection; others stood higher up behind shields. Even within one battery, gun crews had different degrees of protection. The main mountings and their ammunition supply arrangements also belonged to an earlier generation than those of later Japanese battleships.

Amidships, the side was protected by a thick armoured belt: up to 457 mm according to the reference. This did not mean that every part of the ship had that thickness, or that Yashima was twice as well protected as Hatsuse with her 229 mm belt. Materials, the area covered and the entire protection scheme differed. Yashima’s armament allowed her to fight alongside newer ships, but shared 12-inch guns did not erase the differences between them.

sections.title: Blockading the Russian fortress
paragraphs: At the start of the war, Yashima formed part of the main Japanese fleet. Her guns had a clear purpose: to oppose the Russian squadron alongside the other battleships. The threat from that squadron did not disappear after the first night’s torpedo attack. Japanese ships had to return to Port Arthur, watch its approaches and maintain the blockade while the Russians repaired damaged vessels and prepared further sorties.

In May, Yashima operated in Rear Admiral Nashiba’s force with Hatsuse and Shikishima. The Russian Amur laid mines across the blockading ships’ usual route. On 2 (15) May, two battleships were damaged. Early Japanese reports included suggestions of torpedoes and submarines. Later reconstruction distinguishes those anxious explanations from the minefield the force had actually entered.

sections.title: Trying to tow the damaged hull to safety
paragraphs: Yashima did not disappear immediately after striking a mine. Her crew tried to control the flooding, assisted by accompanying vessels. The battleship was then taken in tow—pulled on a cable by another ship—in an attempt to reach safety. But water continued to enter. Remaining afloat did not yet mean that the hull could be brought to a repair base.

The Japanese Combined Fleet’s war diary is particularly valuable here. The extract published by the archive describes Yashima’s slow withdrawal eastward, followed by news that all personnel had left the ship. Kasagi, Suma and Tatsuta are named nearby as providing support. This is evidence that people were taken off; it does not by itself provide a complete list of wounded. Later that day, the battleship sank. She cannot be counted as a ship that disappeared instantly on first touching a mine.

sections.title: The ship was lost before the news became public
paragraphs: Captain Sakamoto Hajime, who commanded Yashima, survived her loss. By the summer of 1905, an American naval journal was reporting his involvement in raising the Russian Bayan at Port Arthur. This concerns the captain’s later work, rather than further service by his former ship: Yashima was never raised, renamed or returned to the fleet. Saving the crew and saving the ship were different outcomes of the rescue effort.

News of the loss followed its own course. The January 1905 issue of Proceedings still discussed persistent rumours that Japanese authorities had neither publicly confirmed nor denied. It even gave the wrong month for the sinking. In early June 1905, a report from Tokyo on disclosed naval losses explicitly named Yashima; the Southland Times printed it on 3 June. A newspaper’s publication date must therefore not be mistaken for the date the ship sank. Yashima was already absent from the line at the Yellow Sea and Tsushima. The mine operation off Port Arthur had ended her service many months before Japan’s victorious campaign concluded.
